metadata.title: Selling Domains Using The Dan.com Outbound Method with Alex Verdea
metadata.author: kickstartcommerce
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to the Kickstart Commerce podcast where we share search marketing and domain investing strategies to help grow your business.

In today's episode, our guest is Alex Verdea, a long time domain investor, the founder of the AudiencePortal.com Domain Marketplace, and author of the recently released book for domain investors: The Domain Investing Playbook.

Today Alex and I:

Discuss which industries are hot and not, and prime for domain investors since the emergence of COVID-19.

How he’s perfected and perfecting increased domain sales discreetly using Dan.com as an outbound tool and customer relationship management system.

We then discuss how he overcomes objections during the domain negotiation process, and how it led him to close a deal after 32 attempts.

And last but not least, Alex shares why and how domain investors should get their hands on his latest book The Domain Investing Playbook.

In closing, don’t forget to subscribe as you enjoy this week's episode via iTunes, GooglePlay, Stitcher, or however you desire to listen. 😍
 
Last but not least, please visit KickstartCommerce.com and DNAdverts.com to learn more about search marketing and domain investing ideas to grow your business.

Andrew Rosener (@andrewrosener) is the founder and CEO of MediaOptions, which has been the #1 domain broker in the world for the last six consecutive years. Since 2008, Andrew has been involved in more than $600 million dollars in domain sales and has played a pivotal role in numerous high-profile domain-name transactions, including X.com to Elon Musk, Zoom.com to Zoom, and Prime.com and Podcast.com to Amazon, as well as thousands of others. 

Andrew is an inductee of the Domain Name Hall of Fame; he was named Domain Investor of the Year by TRAFFIC; and he is the creator of the Rosener Equation, a formula for objectively valuing domain names, widely adopted by the industry.

Andrew is also the owner of DomainSherpa.com, the industry’s leading educational podcast. 

Please enjoy!

It used to be 28, maybe it's 23, maybe it's 18, but it's 20, 28 percent click-through rate just for being the organic first listing of that. Okay, so let's just say roughly speaking, there's a hundred thousand people a month searching for this keyword. 28 percent of those paid, let's say 25 free easy numbers because I'm doing public math, which is generally a rule I have against doing, but 25 percent of those people are going to click. So now you've got 25 thousand people that are going to come to your website, and how many of those people are you going to reasonably convert? And I like to use two percent. I think it's generally a conservative e-commerce metric, two to four percent, but let's say two percent. So you're going to have about 500 people per month that are converting. And then you multiply that by whatever you would have been. It's basically the opportunity cost. So what would you have been paying Google to get that? Okay. And that's going to tell you the cost of customer acquisition to be that number one position in Google. And then based on a bunch of studies from Microsoft, and we can reference those studies in your show notes if you want, but you can demonstrate what the delta is between having a domain name that clearly — it needs to be one of two things. It needs to be a brand that people trust and/or recognize. Or it needs to have clear intent baked in. So the domain name needs to match the intent of the user. And if you have those two things, you're going to materially increase — I don't remember the exact number offhand, but it's a very material increase in the conversion rate and the click-through rate, both. So using that formula, we can demonstrate very clearly the delta between your cost of customer acquisition on joeysbagofdonuts.com versus donuts.com. You're going to have the higher click-through rate, which is going to give you the bigger opportunity, and then you're going to have a higher conversion rate, which is going to obviously grow your business. And so that delta extrapolated out by whatever that reasonable business multiple is the objective value of the domain name. Does that make sense? Tim Ferriss: It does make sense. I think I'd probably need to see it on paper. Andrew Rosener: So ultimately, we're taking it back to that first principle, which is a domain name’ss value is its ability to arbitrage your cost of customer acquisition. If we can reduce your cost of customer acquisition with this domain name, there's a value. And then you just have to multiply that value out by however long you feel is appropriate for your business to tell you what is this domain name worth to your business. And that is a non-trivial, non-objectionable business case that ultimately is what led to my success in this business was I was able to make a business case and convert people where others failed. Because it was a mathematical valuation methodology that nobody had ever seen before. And you could say, "Look, how can you say no? I'm showing you how I'm going to reduce your cost of customer acquisition, which is one of the most important metrics any business is going to measure. And so if I can do that, how many months multiple are you willing to pay me?" Tim Ferriss: I guess, the months multiple is where it seems like you could have a disagreement. Andrew Rosener: Sure, absolutely. And that's where the disagreement lies. But it certainly doesn't have a hundred percent hit rate. Most people still have an emotional block to, "I'm not going to pay some domain squatters X amount of money for this domain name." It's just an emotional wall. And sometimes I can break through that and sometimes I can't. Over long periods of time, I'm generally pretty good at converting people. But once it clicks for people that there is a material reduction in the cost of a customer acquisition, I don't need closed deal on that day. It's like the movie Inception, the Leonardo DiCaprio movie. Once I've planted the seed in your mind, you're going to go home and you're going to go to bed, you're going to have board meetings, you're going to meet with your founders, you're going to meet with teams in your company, and at some point it's going to come up and you're going to wake up one morning with this moment of inception where you think it's your idea that you're going to be able to scale your business in a way that you otherwise wouldn't be able to. You're going to launch a new division, you're going to start buying paid advertising. Some initiative is going to benefit tremendously by owning this domain name. Maybe a new competitor has launched. Maybe there's somebody with your brand name in a different industry that you don't want them to have the domain, but something is going to pop. There's going to come a moment — which is why domain names are generally a very long sales cycle, but there's going to be an inception point where you wake up one morning and you think, "Okay, now I need this domain name." And then you're going to call me back, or you're going to send me an email and you're going to say, "Hey, is that domain still available?" And sometimes it is, sometimes it's not. Another sort of powerful phrase that we've coined is off the market forever. Once these things sell, they're generally off the market forever. The moment a company makes a decision to acquire this domain name that they were fighting tooth and nail not to buy previously, it's basically priceless to them. Because what they then say, which is so interesting to me because they don't realize it before buying it, is that they then say, "But this is my brand." And you go, well, "I couldn't agree more, but then why didn't you want to buy it in the first place?" But the moment a company buys it, the first thing they'll tell you is, "This is my brand. I can't sell it." I won't use this specific example, but we sold the domain. It was quite a good price, but I was fighting tooth and nail. Nobody wanted to buy this domain. It was a very good domain. The price was very good. It was $250,000 for a domain that I would tell you was worth at least double, triple that. And we finally sold it. And immediately, literally 24 hours later, I would say the David versus the Goliath, the David shows up and says, "You know what? I made a mistake. I want to buy it." And said, "I just sold it." And so this guy was really, really successful, but he was like a ninja versus a big Goliath. He was like the Charlie Tuna versus the big factory. But he had a really successful business and he had some money. And he said, "Look, offer them..." I think it was — like the example, I think it was a hundred thousand dollars more. Owner said no. And this guy had just bought it. He hadn't done a single thing with the domain name. It literally hit his account 24 hours ago. He hasn't set up an email on it. He hasn't even redirected the domain name. It's got a parking page on it, nothing, zero. He just is now the owner. And we went from — he bought it for 250. This guy offered 350. He said no. Went to 500. He said no. Went to 750. He said no. Went to $1 million. He said no. That guy tapped out. And this guy was just like, "I don't think there's a price. It would basically be he'd have to buy my whole business for me to sell this domain because this is my brand." And it's a very strange phenomena where people don't — they don't make that click before buying the domain. And the moment they own it, they realize how powerful this is for their brand. It's the most important asset in many cases, not in all cases, but in many cases it's much more valuable and much more powerful than their trademark itself. Because he who has the dot com, there's only one. And so Apple wouldn't be — if it was Applecomputer.com, they couldn't run around calling themselves Apple because somebody else would own Apple. And they would be Apple because the dot com is ingrained into people's brains with trillions and trillions and trillions of dollars in advertising since 1985 when the first domain name was registered. It is just an endless — every sports game has domain names pasted around the arena. Every news channel, you're getting inundated with dot coms, every big brand that you know, it is just ingrained. It's assumed. And so if you are anything except your exact brand match dot com, you cannot or should not refer to yourself as your, let's say, raw brand. If you're dot net or dot io or dot AI even, I would argue, and you're not calling yourself — let's say you're, I'll use Dharmesh because he's a good sport. Dharmesh from HubSpot. He has agent.ai. It's a new little venture that he's launched. And you can't call yourself Agent unless you've got agent.com, because — Tim Ferriss: Why not? Just to — Andrew Rosener: Because people are going to assume you're dot com. If you're agent.ai, then your brand is agent.ai. And if you refer to yourself as anything else, at a minimum, you're going to lose 10 percent of your traffic. This has been done. The best study is from Overstock. Overstock tried to do a rebrand to o.co. That's a whole super phenomenal, interesting story that comes back to the one letter dot coms and whatnot. But anyways, they tried to do a rebrand to o.co, and they were obsessed with this, and they'd made an enormous campaign, and they did massive branding, massive advertising to promote this rebrand. And they immediately — I don't remember, I think it was like six months, maybe less, they immediately pivoted back to overstock.com because what they saw was that they were losing, I think it was 40 percent, it's like 30 to 40 percent of all their traffic was getting lost. Tim Ferriss: And why didn't they just redirect Overstock.com to o.co? Is that a dumb question? Andrew Rosener: Well, no, the point was that they're out there advertising themselves as Overstock is now O, but then people type in o.com. Tim Ferriss: Oh, I see what you're saying. I see what you mean. Andrew Rosener: And so then it's a dead website. So what does that say about your brand. Like, "Oh, I am on a 404 page, or I'm on a dead — this domain doesn't resolve page." This domain doesn't resolve, so it's very detrimental to your brand. I think Amazon highlights this best. I don't know what the increase in conversion rate was, but like just by taking away one step and making the one click purchase had a profound impact on conversion for Amazon. Tim Ferriss: Say that one more time please. Andrew Rosener: When Amazon introduced the one click purchasing — Tim Ferriss: Oh, sure. Andrew Rosener: — it had a profound impact. I remember at the time they were talking about it like these very small — if you can remove just even very small incremental elements of friction between your customer in their journey to close, every small bit of friction that you can remove you're materially increasing your conversion rate, and obviously top line and bottom line. Tim Ferriss: As demonstrated by the number of Amazon boxes that arrive based on my 3:00 AM orders that I think are 100 percent important and critical to my lifestyle. So ultimately that's what a domain does. That's why Amazon bought prime.com, because when I use prime.com, like every time I want to watch something on Prime I go to prime.com. I don't go to Amazon and then click on Prime, and then go to Prime video. Like there's five steps there. Instead I just hit prime.com. Tim Ferriss: You know, this is my one opportunity to share I think the only domain trivia that I have with someone who knows domain a thousand times better than I do, and I'm sure you know this already, but do you know which .com forwards to amazon.com that — Andrew Rosener: I know a lot of them. I sold most of them to them. Tim Ferriss: Did you sell relentless.com? Andrew Rosener: No. No Relentless was actually going to be the original name for Amazon. That was Jeff Bezos' original domain name for the venture actually before pivoting to Amazon. Yeah. But Jeff loves domain names. Tim Ferriss: I'm sure. Andrew Rosener: When he was running the company, when he was still CEO, they bought a lot of domain names. We sold them a lot of domain names, and very strategic and very smart, he understood domain names in a very profound way that most other business executives don't. And I can tell you that with quite a strong basis because I literally have done business with virtually all of them, all of the big companies, and very few understand how a domain name can solve that customer journey the way that Jeff did. And he utilized a lot of those domains. He was way ahead of the curve. He bought podcast.com, which forwards now to Audible. He bought author.com, prime.com, tube.com. Tim Ferriss: He's a smart man. Andrew Rosener: Yeah. Very. A very smart guy. Tim Ferriss: Very ahead of the curve.

metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to this episode of Kickstart Commerce podcast where we interview Yogi Solanki, an India-based domain investor and newcomer to domain investing having discovered how to successfully outbound daily domain sales

In today’s episode, Yogi and I discuss:

Why and what led to his entry into domain investing

How he sold 5 domains the first 45 days of his domain investing journey

The factors and attributes he considers when buying domain names

And last but least, his keys to success for outbound marketing domain names

In closing, don’t forget to subscribe as you enjoy this week's episode via iTunes, GooglePlay, Stitcher or how ever you desire to listen. 😍
 
Last but not least, please visit KickstartCommerce.com and DNAdverts.com to learn more about search marketing and domain investing ideas to grow your business.

to improve your website speed, security, and reliability.

before getting started with Cloudflare.
Here are five things you need to know
before using Cloudflare.
The first thing you need to know before using Cloudflare
is that Cloudflare is not web hosting.
This can be a common point of confusion among beginners
but Cloudflare is not a replacement for web hosting.
You still need a web server to point Cloudflare to.
What this means is that your domain points to Cloudflare
and Cloudflare manages your domain's DNS records
and then points people to the final destination.
If you have the Cloudflare proxy enabled
for a particular DNS record
Cloudflare will store select website files
on their Content Delivery Network.
They're essentially going to pick the most important files
like the style sheet and certain images
and things that take a while to make the page load.
They'll store them on their wide server network
across the world.
Your website will then load more efficiently
because Cloudflare will send the visitor's computer
to the closest server geographically to them.
Since Cloudflare has such a big server network,
that's likely almost always going to be
closer than where your web server is located.
In other words, Cloudflare can kind of start preloading
certain website files faster than if the computer
had to go all the way to the main web server
and back for every single file.
However, just because Cloudflare stores
some of your website's files does not make it web hosting.
You still need a hosting account with a provider
of your choice to get started with Cloudflare.
The second thing they know before using Cloudflare
is that Cloudflare is free to use.
When new users go to sign up,
I'll often get comments or messages saying,
"Christian, Cloudflare is expecting me to pay $20 a month
to sign up.
Are you sure they didn't remove their free plan?"
And no, Cloudflare didn't remove their free plan.
It's a little bit confusing, but when you're signing up,
you have to scroll past the paid plans
and the box for the free plan is under the main columns
for the paid plan.
It's there, scroll down, you'll find it.
Then you can click it and continue with the setup process.
And trust me, for the majority of users,
there's no advantage to upgrading.
Cloudflare's paid plans are for advanced
and enterprise users, so if you're a small business owner
or individual, you can get an insane value
out of the free plan.
I prefer to use Cloudflare on as many websites as I can
because it's just that good.
It will often make your website faster
and their CDN is very valuable to me.
Another thing that you never have to pay for
is hitting that subscribe button.
If you're enjoying my content,
click Subscribe and hit the bell,
so you're the first to know when I release new videos.
The third thing you need to know before using Cloudflare
is that it's not for beginners, but it is simple to learn.
This is similar to what I've said
about WordPress on my channel.
Cloudflare has a learning curve,
and really I mean learning and understanding the process
of manually managing your domain's DNS records.
If you're already familiar with DNS management,
Cloudflare is nothing special and you'll feel right at home.
But if you don't even know what DNS means,
you'll definitely benefit from learning the fundamentals
of DNS management to best succeed with Cloudflare.
Understanding DNS management is not difficult
and I have an entire tutorial on setting up Cloudflare
that I'll link in the description below.
Additionally, most platforms have helpful guides
for setting up DNS records to point to their services.
Think Wix, Squarespace, and Shopify.
Just understand that if it's your first time
doing DNS management, you may make some mistakes
and need to do some troubleshooting
in order to get everything working properly.
The fourth thing to know about Cloudflare
is that it speeds up and protects your website.
These benefits mainly apply if you have the Cloudflare proxy
enabled for A records and C names,
which I would recommend doing in most cases.
The Cloudflare CDN caches common website files
across their global network of servers.
These website files then load from the server
geographically closest to the visitor
and this improves site load times.
Cloudflare has servers in over 300 cities,
including Nashville, where I'm based.
They even have a data center in Hawaii.
Many people don't realize how powerful
such a widespread DNS network is
for the viewer of your website.
Geography does play a big factor in website load times
and Cloudflare cuts down the impact
that your web server location has on your visitors.
The proxy is great for improving load times,
but it also has additional security benefits.
Cloudflare's network automatically screens all visitors
and displays a CAPTCHA
to any traffic suspected of being malicious.
Since so many websites use the Cloudflare proxy,
Cloudflare knows which IP addresses belong to bad actors.
Then, if those IP addresses try to visit your website,
they can preemptively block them before an incident occurs.
And the fifth thing you need to know before using Cloudflare
is that it can do much more than just DNS.
The Cloudflare network provides powerful DDoS protection
and Cloudflare even offers free SSL certificates.
It's actually been my go-to solution
to avoid buying SSL certificates for years.
It's the biggest reason I tell people
not to pay for an SSL certificate.
Just get a free one from Cloudflare instead.
You can also set up email forwarding on your domain
and Cloudflare's implementation is rock solid reliable.
I messed around
with other email forwarding services in the past
and I've had issues with email deliverability and speed.
Sometimes it takes an extra hour or two
before an email reaches the final destination.
They get stuck in the forwarding system,
but that's not gonna be a problem at Cloudflare.
All the emails are forwarded instantly
and it's another free benefit.
Cloudflare can also obfuscate your contact email address
on your website in the event that bot traffic is detected.
This prevents bots from visiting your website
just to scrape your email address and send you spam mail
and it's one of those benefits
you're not really gonna be able to quantify
because we all get spam mail
from a bunch of different sources.
But having this feature is going to cut down
on the amount of bots that scrape your email
and put it on some list somewhere,
and that's ultimately gonna mean
that you get less spam mail.
These are just a few of the many bonus features
included in Cloudflare, even in the free plan.
So if you have a WordPress website,
using Cloudflare is a no-brainer.
And even if you're using a simpler website builder like Wix,
Squarespace or Shopify,
I'm still an advocate of using Cloudflare
for DNS management.
Some platforms and web hosts may offer Cloudflare built in
and this is a great way to take advantage
of the Cloudflare CDN
without having to understand manual DNS management.
However, to take advantage of every Cloudflare feature,
like email forwarding, you do have to set it up manually
through Cloudflare.com.
So I think it's worth investing the time
to learn DNS management and set it up that way.
I have an entire tutorial video

segments.text: Hello everybody, welcome to PMN online.
Here I will show you how to add DNS
records on Cloudflare. Let's start by
understanding why this process is so
important. Whether you're launching a
brand new website or adjusting the
settings of an existing one, managing
DNS records is essential for a stable
and fully functional online presence.
DNS or domain name system is like the
phone book of the internet. It
translates domain names into IP
addresses, allowing browsers to load
internet resources. If your DNS settings
are incorrect, it can lead to website
downtime or functionality issues. So,
it's crucial to get these settings
right. Now, let's dive into the
step-by-step process of adding DNS
records on Cloudflare. First things
first, you'll need to log into your
Cloudflare account. Think of this as
your command center where you control
all aspects of your domain settings.
Once you're logged in, you'll want to
select the domain you intend to manage.
This is particularly important if you
have multiple domains under your
account. Always make sure you're working
on the correct domain to prevent any
unwanted changes. After selecting your
domain, look towards the top of the
Cloudflare interface. You will see a
section labeled DNS. By navigating here,
you're entering the hub where all DNS
configurations take place. It's in this
section that you'll see a list of
existing DNS records. These records are
crucial as they dictate various aspects
of your domain's connectivity and
overall functionality. When you're ready
to add a new DNS record, you'll notice
an add record button. Click on this
button to begin setting up the new
record. Starting from here, you can
input the specific settings required for
your domain or any subdomains you might
have. Let's move on to configuring this
new record. The first decision you'll
make is selecting the type of record you
need. Common options include A, a AAA,
CNAME, MX, TXT, among others. Each type
serves a unique purpose. For example, an
A record is used for pointing a domain
to an IP address, while a CNAME can be
used to alias one name to another.
Understanding which type suits your
needs is key to effective DNS
management. Next, we'll need to fill in
the name field. This is essentially the
host part of your domain. For the root
domain, you can use the at symbol, or
you can specify a subdomain like www or
mail to target specific areas of your
site. Now, let's talk about the content
field. This is where you'll enter the
destination for your DNS record. It
could be an IP address, a host name, or
sometimes a value for verification, like
a TXT record. Accuracy is critical here
to ensure your DNS settings function as
intended. The TTL or time to live is
another important setting. This dictates
how long the record is cached by DNS
resolvers. For most users, leaving this
as auto is sufficient as it defaults to
Cloudflare's optimal caching time.
Finally, let's discuss the proxy status
option. This is specific to A, AAA, and
CNAME records. Here you decide whether
to enable Cloudflare's proxy feature,
which is denoted by an orange cloud, or
to set it as DNS only, indicated by a
gray cloud. The proxy feature enhances
security and performance. So, weigh your
needs before making a decision. Once
you've input all the necessary
information and you're confident
everything is accurate, click the save
button to create your DNS record. If
there are no errors, your new DNS record
will be successfully added. And there
you have it, a comprehensive guide to
adding DNS records on Cloudflare.
Remember, DNS changes might take a few
minutes to propagate, so patience is
key. This skill is an integral part of
managing your domains effectively.
Hopefully, you now have a better
understanding of how to add DNS records
on Cloudflare. For more step-by-step
tutorials and guides, subscribe to KMN
Online and never miss an update.

The first decision you'll make is selecting the type of record you need. Common options include A, a AAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, among others. Each type serves a unique purpose. For example, an A record is used for pointing a domain to an IP address, while a CNAME can be used to alias one name to another. Understanding which type suits your needs is key to effective DNS management. Next, we'll need to fill in the name field. This is essentially the host part of your domain. For the root domain, you can use the at symbol, or you can specify a subdomain like www or mail to target specific areas of your site. Now, let's talk about the content field. This is where you'll enter the destination for your DNS record. It could be an IP address, a host name, or sometimes a value for verification, like a TXT record. Accuracy is critical here to ensure your DNS settings function as intended. The TTL or time to live is another important setting. This dictates how long the record is cached by DNS resolvers. For most users, leaving this as auto is sufficient as it defaults to Cloudflare's optimal caching time. Finally, let's discuss the proxy status option. This is specific to A, AAA, and CNAME records. Here you decide whether to enable Cloudflare's proxy feature, which is denoted by an orange cloud, or to set it as DNS only, indicated by a gray cloud. The proxy feature enhances security and performance. So, weigh your needs before making a decision. Once you've input all the necessary information and you're confident everything is accurate, click the save button to create your DNS record. If there are no errors, your new DNS record will be successfully added. And there you have it, a comprehensive guide to adding DNS records on Cloudflare. Remember, DNS changes might take a few minutes to propagate, so patience is key. This skill is an integral part of managing your domains effectively. Hopefully, you now have a better understanding of how to add DNS records on Cloudflare. For more step-by-step tutorials and guides, subscribe to KMN Online and never miss an update.

metadata.title: S2 E8 The $500 Domain Investing Challenge: Who’s Winning & What We’ve Learned So Far
metadata.author: GoDaddy Domain Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of the Domain Academy Podcast DREAM Contest, we edge closer to the grand finale of our year-long, $500 domain investing challenge! Host Joe Styler is joined by top participants Mike Cyger, Andrew Alleman, and Piyush Patel for an honest roundtable on the critical strategies, lessons, and surprises that have defined this unique experiment in domain flipping and digital asset investing.

Find out who's in the lead, how strategies have shifted, and what worked (and didn’t) as each investor shares real-world results and actionable tips—perfect for both newcomers and seasoned domain pros.

• Track our leaderboard: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1-y2hm89miTikAL5s0hVipL_fMfBYfkKnBR44jhOWKl8/edit?pli=1&gid=410596151
• Watch all episodes: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL4Fk98QgRw5iRGKCFpW9JSSGTm1yFmY8P
• Listen to the podcast: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-domain-academy-podcast/id1779312301
• Follow us on X: https://x.com/dnacademy

Special thanks to our regulars for their willingness to share wins, misses, and creative approaches to research, pricing, and outreach—plus thoughts on volume vs. selectivity, common new investor mistakes, and why networking often beats waiting for inbound offers.

 Want to level up your own domaining game? Explore exclusive Domain Academy classes, proprietary tools, and membership options at https://domainacademy.com?utm_source=podcast&utm_medium=desc&utm_campaign=DA

Mentioned in this episode:
• GoDaddy Auctions - Auctions.GoDaddy.com
• Domain Discount Club Pro: https://www.godaddy.com/domains/discount-domain-club?utm_source=YouTube&utm_medium=video-description&utm_campaign=DDC-Pro

• NamePros.com, Discord, Atom.com, ExpiredDomains.net, and more
Interested in joining our next season or getting live help from mentors? Leave a comment, or email jstyler@godaddy.com.

Remember to always do your own research and that these videos are provided for educational and informational purposes only and do not constitute investment or financial advice. Always do your own research.

metadata.title: Domain investing: Using DotDB to find end users and value domains
metadata.author: Andrew Allemann
metadata.shortDescription:
How many TLDs is a domain registered in? Here's how to find out and what it really means.

In this video, I walk through how domain investors use DotDB to check how many top level domains (TLDs) a second level domain (SLD) is registered in, which is a key signal of demand and potential value.

You’ll learn:

-How to use DotDB to pull this data in bulk
- Why the raw numbers can be misleading
- How to dig deeper by evaluating the actual websites using those domains
- How to spot potential end users who might upgrade to your domain

Want more insights like this? Visit https://domainnamewire.com

Whether you want to flip a single domain or a portfolio of domains, this video is for you. We'll walk you through the process, from identifying a domain that you want to flip, to finding the right buyer, to completing the sale. Watch and learn how to flip a domain for 10,000 – 1 million dollars!

From strategy to tactics, you'll be able to flip a domain like a pro. And if you're successful, you'll not only make a lot of money, but you'll also learn a lot about domain marketing in the process! So come join us as we take you step-by-step through the process of flipping a domain for 10,000 – 1 million dollars!

metadata.title: S1E6 A Chat with the Boss GoDaddy's VP of Domain Investing Paul Nicks
metadata.author: GoDaddy Domain Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Season 1 Episode 6 
We end this mini-series with a chat with the person we call the boss. Paul Nicks is the Vice President of Domain Investors at GoDaddy, and oversees a division dedicated to serving domain name investors. Paul joins us to talk about his experience in the industry, how GoDaddy can help domain investors thrive, plus a look at the future of domain investing. 

GoDaddy’s Domain Academy miniseries dives into the lucrative world of domain investing with lead instructor Joe Styler and community manager James Iles. In this 6-episode series, unlock pro tips on valuing, buying, and selling domain names. Featuring 5 special guests, we’ll guide you through the essentials to set yourself up for success, whether you’re a newbie or a seasoned investor.

For more information, tools, and training check us out at https://www.DomainAcademy.com?utm_source=YouTube-Podcast&utm_medium=YouTube&utm_campaign=YouTube_Podcast.

**These podcasts are provided for educational and informational purposes only and do not constitute investment or financial advice. Always do your own research.**

metadata.title: Domain Name Investing 101 with Peter Askew - Founder of Deep South Ventures
metadata.author: POWERS Pod
metadata.shortDescription:
Peter Askew runs a bootstrapped, .com domain development business (often solo). He typically sources domains from the expired aftermarket and uses their descriptive nature as inspiration for each venture.

Current projects: VidaliaOnions.com | RanchWork.com | DudeRanch.com

On this episode Chris & Peter discuss:

Investing in domains 101 and why ".com" is king
How to build job boards & why they're so valuable
How to build businesses from purchased domains

Key Takeaways:
(2:05) - How did you become a failed domain investor?

(6:42) - What does “building a project” mean in your world?

(13:30) - How would a common person find these domain marketplaces?

(16:36) - How do you value Domains?

(21:47) - How did you get from buying a domain for onions to actually selling the onions?

(27:05) - Why aren’t you in a hurry to grow the business?

(28:30) - The domain industry

(31:24) - What makes an amazing domain investor?

(33:15) - Can I simply license out domain names?

(37:21) - Can people hack and steal domain names?

(39:04) - Does AI or Web3 disrupt this space?

(40:37) - What’s the most valuable domain name in the industry?

(42:14) - Do you have to have a site in order to monetize a domain?

(45:47) - How would you build a job board for an industry from scratch?

metadata.title: How I Made $10 Million Trading Domains
metadata.author: Manic Millionaire
metadata.shortDescription:
How did I make $10 million trading domain names?

In Day 3 of the Manic Millionaire vlog, I’m in Hiroshima, Japan, sharing the thinking behind my domain business.

I talk through my three-bucket strategy, how I approach high-frequency domain trading, and where I see opportunities in the domain market. It’s an insight into how I buy, hold and sell domains, and how those decisions fit together.

If you’re curious about domain investing or already building a portfolio, this episode gives you a closer look at my approach.

Subscribe to follow the daily vlogs, domain deals and what I’m building next.

#ManicMillionaire #DomainInvesting #DomainNames

Two-thirds of the year is in the books, and what a year it has been. Technology is changing quickly, and this is impacting the domain business.

  

 On today’s show, I discuss my domain results so far this year and dig into some of the changes I’m making to my investing. I also discuss how I’m using the GoDaddy Auctions API to make bidding easier. 

 Also: .Net prices, GoValue, Radix, Unstoppable [Domains], D3, and more

 Sponsor: Sav.com backorders

metadata.title: The Reality of Owning a Domain Flipping Business
metadata.author: Ownerly
metadata.shortDescription:
How does the domain flipping business actually work? See how a $10 investment turns into $12,500 through digital real estate.

Behind every profitable domain name is a process of identifying value, holding assets, and finding the right buyer. While the potential for high returns exists, the reality involves years of persistence and steady effort. Many participants start with modest gains, earning small amounts per month while waiting for the right market opportunity to strike.

Success in this field requires more than just picking catchy strings of letters. It demands patience to manage a portfolio, the discipline to handle self-employment challenges, and the insight to recognize when an asset has appreciated. We explore the economics of digital assets, the risks of long-term holding, and what it takes to scale from a single purchase to a significant payout.

Because in the domain flipping business, the real profit isn't just in the sale. It is in the years of diligent work that make the sale possible.

Subscribe for weekly business model breakdowns, and comment which industry you want to see analyzed next.

Not the person chasing every trending keyword.
The survivors fall into a few recognizable categories.
There are the people who treat it as
a long-term side portfolio, funded by a

-flipping business.

long game.

Research subscriptions, hosting for your landing pages, a CRM, or at least a disciplined email setup, and marketplace listing fees add up to a few hundred to a couple thousand dollars a year. The third fixed cost, the one that's easiest to ignore, is your own time. Domain investing is not passive in the way people imagine. Hunting for names, evaluating comparables, negotiating with buyers who go quiet for three weeks and then come back with an insulting offer, handling transfers, and managing expiration dates takes wheel hours. If you value those hours at even $20 each, and you spend 10 hours a week on this, you've invested over $10,000 of unpaid labor annually in a business that might pay you nothing. Then come the variable costs, which only show up when you succeed, and that's the cruel irony. When a domain sells, a marketplace broker might take 15%. If you sell through an intermediary or broker, expect 20%. Escrow fees take another few percent. If you're outbound marketing to end users, cold emailing companies that might want the name, you're burning time, and sometimes paying for lead lists and outreach tools. And in the background, there are taxes. In most jurisdictions, income from domain sales is either ordinary income or capital gains, depending on how the tax authority classifies you. And if you're doing this frequently, you're usually deemed a dealer, which means ordinary income and potentially self-employment tax. There's also what I'd call the invisible operating expense. Opportunity cost and attrition. Domains don't age like wine. A name built around a trend, a buzzword, or a technology fad can lose most of its value in 18 months. Remember when everyone bought names with the word crypto or metaverse or NFT in them? Those portfolios cost real money to renew, while their value evaporated. In this business, your inventory is perishable, and you don't know it's spoiled until you've already paid to keep it on the shelf. So if the business is this brutal, how does anyone actually make money? Here's the counterintuitive secret, and it's the thing that separates the survivors from the people who quit after 18 months. The profit engine in domain investing is not volume of sales. It's the power law distribution of outcomes. In a typical successful portfolio, one or two names generate the overwhelming majority of the revenue, often more than 80%. The rest are essentially paying the rent for the chance to own those few winners. This is exactly how venture capital works. A venture fund doesn't win because every investment succeeds. It wins because one investment returns a hundred times its cost, and that single result covers all the failures and still delivers a profit. Domain investing is venture capital for people with four-figure budgets and no board of directors. That means the survival strategy is not finding the next million-dollar name. It's controlling your cost basis so you can afford to hold a wide enough portfolio for long enough to catch the occasional outlier. The investors who last are the ones who keep their renewal costs low, buy names at deeply discounted prices through expiring auctions and drop catches, avoid fads, and critically, price their names for the end user, not the fellow investor. A domain sold to another investor typically fetches a wholesale price. A domain sold to a business that will actually build a brand on it can fetch 10 to 100 times more. The entire game is moving names from the wholesale market to the retail market and finding the rare buyer who has a budget, a need, and no other option. Smart sellers also learn to make the price easier to swallow. A small company that can't write a single $12,000 check might happily commit to a payment plan, a few hundred dollars a month for three years, with the domain held in escrow until the final installment clears. Lease-to-own deals turn a name that would never have sold into a steady stream of income, and they let the buyer start building a brand on it right away. It's slower money, but it converts stubborn inventory into cash flow, which is precisely what a leaky bucket means. The second part of the secret is patience measured in years, not months. Many of the best sales happen on names held for 5, 8, even 12 years. The investor who survives is the one who could afford to wait, which means the real moat in this business is cheap holding costs and a day job that pays the bills while the portfolio matures. Almost no one makes this a full-time income in the first few years, and the ones who tell you otherwise are usually selling a course. Let's put numbers on this and walk through what a genuinely good year looks like. Imagine an investor with a portfolio of 250 domains. They bought them carefully over four years, averaging about $200 each, so they've got $50 ,000 of capital tied up in inventory. Their annual renewals come to roughly $4,000. Tools and listings cost another $1,500, and they spend maybe $1,000 on legal and accounting. Call it $6,500 in fixed costs for the year. Now suppose this is the year the portfolio finally pays off. They sell eight domains. That's a hit rate of just over 3%, which is genuinely strong. Five of those sales are modest, around $2 ,500 each, totaling $12,500. Two are better at $8,000 each, adding $16,000. And one is the big one, a clean two-word brand that a funded startup decides it can't live without, selling for $35,000. Total gross revenue comes to $63,500. Subtract marketplace commissions and escrow fees, which average about 15%, and you've lost roughly $9,500, leaving about $54,000 in net proceeds. Subtract the $6,500 of fixed costs, and you're at about $47,500. Subtract the $6,500 of fixed costs, and you're at about $47,500. Subtract the original cost basis of the eight domains sold, roughly $1,600, and you land at around $46,000 of pre-tax profit. That's a fantastic year, nearly a 90% return on a $50,000 portfolio. And this is the number that ends up in the screenshots people post online. But look at what that year depended on. It depended on one $35,000 sale. Take that single transaction away, and the revenue drops to $28,500. The net after commissions falls to about $24 ,000. And after fixed costs, the profit is roughly $17,000. Still decent, but now it's a 34% return, and you've done an enormous amount of work for it. And now watch what happens in the year that doesn't cooperate. Same investor, same portfolio, same discipline. But this year, the market cools. Interest rates are high, startup funding dries up, and the buyers who were circling last year have quietly vanished. Instead of eight sales, there are three. Two small ones at $2,200 each and one at $5,000 for total revenue of $9,400. Commissions take about $1,400, leaving $8,000. Fixed costs of $6,500 bring that down to $1,500. Subtract the cost basis of the three names sold, around $600, and you're left with $900 of profit for a year of work, tying up $50,000 of capital. That's under 2%, worse than a savings account, and you've spent hundreds of hours. Now let the dominoes fall. The renewal bill doesn't shrink, but a few names you plan to drop are coming up for renewal at higher prices because the registry raised fees. A couple of the fad names in the portfolio are now clearly dead, which means you've paid renewals on them for nothing. Your tax accountant informs you that because you sold three domains at profit, you owe self -employment tax on income you barely kept. Your research subscription renews automatically, and because it's been a slow year, you lose motivation, stop sending outreach emails, and miss the one inbound inquiry that sat in your inbox for six weeks before the buyer moved on. If that $35,000 buyer from last year had been the only one who came around, you'd have just posted a loss on your books. Add one more cost, say, a trademark dispute over a name you bought without checking, with legal fees of $4,000, and the same venture that earned $46,000 last year now sits at a loss of roughly $3,000, with your unsold inventory slowly depreciating and the clock still ticking on next year's renewals. That's the whole business in two years. Same person, same skills, same portfolio. The difference between a spectacular outcome and a miserable one was the timing of a handful of buyers you never controlled. The spread between those years isn't a bug. It's the entire nature of a power law business, and if you can't stomach that volatility, you will quit just before the sale that would have made it worthwhile. So who actually succeeds in domain flipping? Not the person with a few hundred dollars and a dream. Not the person chasing every trending keyword. The survivors fall into a few recognizable categories. There are the people who treat it as a long-term side portfolio, funded by a stable income, who can hold names for a decade without flinching. There are the specialists, who know a niche so well that they can spot names a particular industry will need before the industry knows it, and who build relationships with those buyers directly. And there are the professionals, who have been doing this since the 90s, who accumulated generic names when they cost almost nothing, and who now harvest them at prices the market has caught up to. What they share is discipline about costs, patience about timing, and an almost boring approach to risk. They don't expect every name to be a winner. They expect most names to lose, and a few to carry the whole portfolio. They know that the business isn't about finding hidden treasure. It's about surviving long enough, cheaply enough, for the treasure to find you. If you're thinking about starting, treat it like a long-shot venture bet, and fund it only with money you can afford to see go quiet for years. Learn trademark law before you spend a dime. Keep your renewals lean. Price for end-users, not for other flippers. Review your portfolio every year, and have the nerve to drop the names that haven't earned a single inquiry, because sentimentality is just another word for a renewal fee. And above all, remember that every domain you register is a small recurring obligation that will outlast your enthusiasm unless you manage it ruthlessly. The beach, the cocktail, the buzzing phone, it happens. But it happens to the people who spent years quietly paying the rent on a portfolio of mostly worthless names, waiting for the one that wasn't. That's the real economics of owning a domain -flipping business. The dream is a payout. The reality is patience, math, and a very long game.

metadata.title: The Truth About Raising Capital In Africa (That Investors Won't Tell You)
metadata.author: Eunice Ajim
metadata.shortDescription:
Master the investor due diligence process to ensure your startup is ready for funding. Learn the steps to pass critical reviews.

Most founders believe the pitch meeting is the final hurdle, but the real work happens afterward. This guide details the six domains investors evaluate, including revenue quality, governance, and cap table structures. We explain how to prepare for the specific questions that determine whether your company receives a term sheet or a rejection.

If you are building an African startup, you must navigate unique challenges like currency risk and regulatory hurdles. We break down these structural barriers and show you how to demonstrate market capture potential to venture-scale investors. Understanding how to present your traction and unit economics clearly is essential for any founder serious about raising capital.

Subscribe for weekly startup strategy breakdowns, and comment which part of the fundraising process you find most challenging.

0:00 What Happens After You Leave the Room
2:44 Evaluating the Team as the Primary Asset
4:17 The Reality of Market Sizing
7:27 Fixing Cap Table Landmines Early
8:40 Navigating Africa-Specific Structural Risks

If you’re a founder preparing to raise, this episode gives you the investor lens you need to move faster and avoid avoidable mistakes.

Keywords:startup fundraising, investor due diligence, African startups, venture capital, founder tips, raising capital, startup advice, seed stage, cap table, unit economics, business model, market sizing

factors that and most due diligence

here's what most founders do not know.

that is the part that determines whether
a check gets written. This episode is
useful whether you are a founder
preparing for a raise, an emerging fund
manager building your own framework, or
an investor who has been doing this
informally and wants a more structured
approach. I'm going to walk through six
domains in the order they actually shape
my assessment. Let me start with the one
I always go to first. Due diligence is
not primarily about finding reasons not
to invest. That is a wrong mental model
and it leads to risk-adverse paralysis,
especially in early-stage African
markets where some imperfections in the
documentations, the team structure, or
the traction curve is almost always
present. Due diligence done correctly is
about building enough understanding of a
company to make a specific prediction,
will this team in this market with this
business model be able to compound the
capital we deploy into something that
returns at least 10x. Everything in the
diligence process is oriented towards
that prediction. Understanding the
investors diligence framework is also
tactically valuable for founders because
it tells you where to invest your
preparation energy. Founders who walk
into a process with organized
documentation, clear answers to the
predictable questions, and a proactive
acknowledgement of the risk, those
founders move faster through diligence.
Speed matters because investors
conviction fades when a process drags.
So, domain one, the team. I start here
because in an early stage company, the
team is the product. The product will
change. The market sizing will be
revised. The business model will
iterate. The team is the most durable
asset in the company at the seed stage.
Here is something I do that most
investors do not talk about. If there
are two co-founders, I ask them each the
same question separately without the
other one in the room. I ask, "What does
your co-founder do that you could not
do?" And I listen for two things, the
specificity of the answer and the
consistency between what each one says
about the other. A co-founder pair that
can describe each other's contribution
precisely and consistently has done the
work of understanding their own
partnership. A co-founder pair where one
person gives a vague answer and the
other gives a very different vague
answer has not. The gap will show up in
the business. In the African context
specifically, I also evaluate, "Does the
team have a operational presence in the
market they are targeting. I visited
Lagos is not the same as I have been
doing sales calls in Lagos for 18
months. The founders who are in the
markets, who have built relationships in
the market, who understand the
regulatory environment and the buyer
behavior from direct experience, those
are the teams that survive the execution
challenges that are unique to building
in Africa. Domain two, the market. The
market question I am answering is not is
this a big market? Because most of the
time it is. Is there a clear path from
where this company is today to capturing
enough of a real market to produce a
venture scale return? I want to give you
the honest reaction to most common
market sizing mistake I see. The first
is typically like top-down total
addressable market. The African tech
market is X billion. We expect 1%. I
stopped reading there. That number tells
me nothing about whether this specific
company can capture meaningful revenue
in a specific segment at this stage. The
market size I care about is built from
the bottom up. How many customers exist
who have this exact problem? What would
they pay for this exact solution? And
does that number at full penetration
produce returns that justify
Building a total addressable market from
the bottom up every time. I also
evaluate market concentration risk. If
80% of this company potential customers
are in one city or in one country, what
happens if a regulatory change, a
currency crisis, or macro shocks hit
that market? And I'm not asking them to
avoid concentration. Sometimes
concentration is often how you get to
scale fastest. I'm asking whether the
team has thought about it and has a
plan. Domain three, traction and unit
economics. Traction means the real
customers paying real money and coming
back. At pre-seed and seed, I expect to
see some signal that the market wants
what this company is building. That
signal can be modest, but it needs to be
real. In African market, unit economics
are particularly telling because the
execution environment is harder. A
company that has healthy unit economic
despite high infrastructure costs,
payment friction, and the cost of
offline distribution, that company is
showing me something genuinely
important. The business [clears throat]
model is structurally sound, not just
favorable under ideal conditions. A
company that has attractive unit
economics only because they have not yet
had to deal with the full cost of
operating at scale, that is a risk I
need to price carefully. Domain four,
business model and revenue quality. Not
all revenue is equal. I'm looking at how
predictable is the revenue stream? How
sticky is it? What is the ratio of
recurring revenue to transactional
revenue? Africa specific consideration,
payment allocation in many African
market is more complex than in more
matured markets. A company with
clean-looking revenue line that has
significant account receivable aging,
where a large portion of their billed
revenue is more than 90 days
uncollected, has a different financial
health profile than a headline number
suggests. Domain five, governance and
legal structure. This is a domain that
most early-stage African founders are
least prepared for. And it's also the
one that most often cause investors
reluctant to proceed, even when the
business is good. This is the governance
question I want to address directly
because it creates more deal friction
than almost any other single issue. Cap
table landmines. Every equity promise
that was made informally, an early
employee you told you would get some
equity, an advisor you said we will work
something out. That promise exists on a
shadow cap table. When a sophisticated
investor legal team runs the diligence,
those promises surface and the close get
delayed or repriced or even killed
because the founder now has to resolve
something they should have formalized a
year ago. Clean the cap table now, not
before series A, right now. I'm not
looking for perfection. I'm looking for
a founder who is honest about what is in
order and what is not and who has a plan
to fix the things that need fixing
before close. Domain six, Africa
specific structural risk. This is the
layer that most standard due diligence
framework do not include. Currency risk.
What is the company's revenue currency
exposure? If the company earns in naira,
cities, Kenyan shillings and has dollar
dominant costs or investors who expect
dollar returns, that gap needs to be
understood and managed, not ignored.
Second is regulatory risk. A business
model that is fully legal in Kenya may
require a different licensing structure
in Nigeria. Founder needs to have done
the regulatory homework in every market
they need operating in. Cross-border
expansion assumptions. Many pitches I
see include a slide showing 10 African
countries the company plans to be in by
year three. I probe that aggressively
because cross-border expansion in Africa
is genuinely difficult. Payment rails,
regulatory requirements, language,
consumer behavior, and the distribution
infrastructure are all different across
every border. The companies that expand
well to do it sequentially and with real
operational presence, not theoretically.
There are things that disqualify
companies in other markets that are
explicitly looked past in early-stage
African investing because penalizing
African founders for them reflects the
assumption of a different ecosystem. I
look past imperfect early financial
records. As long as the founder is
transparent and building towards proper
accounting, I look past a founding team
where one co-founder left the company.
Founder departures are common in
early-stage companies everywhere. What I
do not look past is dishonesty. A
founder who misrepresents their team or
their customer relationship, even once,
is a founder I will not back. I'm
evaluating honesty under pressure
throughout the entire process, not just
in the pitch meeting. Everything you say
during diligence is data. The diligence
process is not an adversarial audit. It
is the beginning of a working
relationship. The founder who treats it
that way, who answer hard questions
directly, who flags issues before I find
them, who show me they can handle
scrutiny. Those are the founders who
move through diligence fastest and who
build the kind of investor relationship
that matters at the moment when things
get hard. If you are a founder preparing
for a raise, run this checklist on
yourself before you go into any investor
meeting. Team, market, traction,
business model, governance, Africa
specific structural risk. If you cannot
answer each domain with specifics, you
are not ready to pitch yet. Spend that
time closing the gaps instead. Drop in
the comments which of the six domain is
the one you are the least prepared for
right now. I want to know where the gaps
actually are. Not the generic version,
the specific ones. Okay, on the next
episode, we're going to look at how to
build a fundable startup when the
infrastructure around you is generally
broken. And until next time,
have a good day.

For nearly as long as the internet has existed, savvy investors have found a way to make a profit by trading in domain names, a practice known as domaining. 

Growing levels of worldwide internet usage, increased demand for short, meaningful domain names, and this decade’s introduction of thousands of new domain extensions make today’s domaining landscape more robust than ever.

Those who are interested in entering today’s internet real estate market and making money with domains can get ahead of the curve by getting a grasp on necessary domaining knowledge.

Whether you plan to start domaining as a side hustle or dream of becoming a domaining titan, we will lay out the basics and provide advice to help you on your domain investing journey.

What is domaining and how can it make you money?
Domaining is generally defined as investing in domain names with the intention of making a profit. A profit is most often realized by selling or leasing a domain for more than you purchased it for. 

A real estate investor hopes to buy a piece of land (i.e., domain name) in order to resell it for a profit or to construct a building (i.e., website) on it to sell products and services. Just as a real estate investor considers various factors in order to determine the value of land, a domainer needs to consider multiple aspects of a domain prior to investing.

Two methods of making money with domain investing
No matter your level of experience online, before you jump into domaining and start building your portfolio you will need an understanding of what domaining looks like today. There are two main methods of making money with domains: short-term investing or “domain flipping,” and long-term domain investing.

Both domaining strategies involve purchasing domain names and building a domain portfolio. How you manage those domain names, though, depends entirely on which investing approach you choose. Traditional domain investing requires less regular attention than flipping, but will also likely take longer to turn a profit.

What to consider before domaining
If domaining sounds exciting to you, that’s great. But before you commit to domain investing, there are a few other things to take into account. Domaining can be satisfying as a part-time venture or long-term career. Which you choose will depend on a few factors:

Time: If you want to invest in domains full time, you will be competing with many other investors who already have domaining experience and proven strategies that have led them to success.
Finding valuable domains and building a strong domain portfolio takes time and research.

Money: When it comes to domaining, you have to invest money to make money. How much you invest will depend on your business model and what kind of domain names you want to invest in, along with how much time you plan to spend optimizing and monetizing your domains.

If you plan to hold a large portfolio of domain names you will incur higher overhead in the form of renewal fees, so you want to make sure you are at least earning enough to cover those fees and the initial acquisition prices.

Competition in your vertical: Remember that domaining is already a popular investment opportunity, and you will be entering what can be considered one of the fastest-growing online side hustles today. 

Before you shape your business plan, look at how many investors are already invested in that segment of the industry and see what domains can be had for good value.

Domaining can be an exciting investment opportunity, but making money with domains requires thorough research, an understanding of what strategy you want to pursue, and a plan of action. With the right tools and plan, anyone can invest in domains.

Domain flipping, also known as domain name flipping, is the practice of buying and selling domain names for profit. It's a lucrative business model where individuals, often referred to as domain resellers, capitalize on the demand for unique and memorable domain names. The process involves acquiring domain names that are undervalued or have potential branding appeal, holding onto them, and then selling them at a higher price.

Many entrepreneurs enter the domain flipping business with the hope of making substantial profits. The concept is simple: find domains that have marketable keywords, short and memorable names, or potential for future businesses, buy them at a reasonable price, and resell them at a premium. While it might seem straightforward, it requires research, patience, and a keen understanding of market trends.

For beginners looking to delve into domain flipping, resources like tutorials and guides are available. These materials offer insights into the art of domain name flipping, explaining strategies to identify valuable domains, negotiate prices, and reach potential buyers. Online platforms like DomainRacer provide a marketplace for buying and selling domains, facilitating the entire process.

Is domain reselling profitable? The answer varies. While some domain flippers have struck gold with high-value sales, success is not guaranteed. It's crucial to stay updated on industry trends, consider the cultural and linguistic relevance of domain names (even in languages like Hindi), and exercise patience as domains might take time to appreciate in value.

In conclusion, domain flipping can be a profitable venture for those who are willing to put in the effort and research. It's a business where creativity, market insight, and a bit of luck can translate into significant financial gains.

metadata.title: How I Turned $10 into $1500 Selling a Domain | Domain Flipping Business Explained
metadata.author: KT Blogger
metadata.shortDescription:
I bought a domain for $10 and sold it for $1,500! In this video, I share my domain flipping story and explain how buying and selling domain names works—even without building a website.

This was a blank domain with DA and DR of 0, sold through the GoDaddy marketplace. I held it for around a year, and the sale happened about one month after listing it. I explain the experience behind this sale and introduce the domain flipping business for beginners who want to understand this online business model.

If you have been wondering how to sell a domain name, what makes a domain valuable, or how people make money selling domains, this video is a starting point. Domain investing involves finding names that could be useful to a business and connecting them with the right buyer. Research, pricing, and patience all play a role.

The $1,500 was the sale price, not net profit after fees and other costs. This is my personal result, and every domain will have different demand and selling potential.

Have you ever bought a domain hoping to sell it later? Share your experience or your biggest domain flipping question in the comments.

Subscribe to KT Blogger for more real business experiences, SEO tips, and practical online business ideas.

Catch Part 1 - how to find great keyword domains, here https://youtu.be/6d5xrStqY-4

Learn why keyword placement matters, how to filter for domains that actually sell, and actionable tips to help you spend less time scrolling and more time bidding on winning names.

Ready for serious domain investing? DomainAcademy.com offers exclusive classes, tools, and resources for pro-level domainers. Plus, check out the GoDaddy Domain Discount Club Pro for powerful savings:
https://www.godaddy.com/domains/discount-domain-club?utm_source=YouTube&utm_medium=video-description&utm_campaign=DDC-Pro

metadata.title: Dynadot: An Often Overlooked Player in the Expired Domain Name Aftermarket
metadata.author: cssfx
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to another episode of SNATCHING WITH SARAH.

I want to talk to you today about a registrar that's been around for a long time but is starting to emerge as a contender in the aftermarket - Dynadot.

One of the coolest features Dynadot has is the ability to delete your domains that you don't want, shortly after registering for a nominal fee.  You have a 120 hour window in which you're given a grace period for deleting domains you've registered in case you no longer want them.  Dynadot only charges you about 2 bucks to delete them and get a refund.

Another nice thing is that they do not fall under the umbrella of Namejet or Snapnames...  Their marketplace now contains pending delete domains that are exclusive to only Dynadot.  And some of these are very good, as their marketplace is not quite as saturated as some of the others yet.

The marketplace has some unique features.  They've utilized verisign's traffic monitoring abilities to give you the estimated monthly traffic on their expired/pre-release domains as well, so you can get a good gauge for how much traffic the domain is actually getting, since we all know how skewed the numbers from Alexa and Compete can be.  I've found these numbers to be pretty consistent with compete.com as well.  Of course the domain traffic on compete is generally displaying a downward slope, and rightfully so given the fact this is most likely an abandoned domain.

Dynadot also has the ability to add prepaid credits to your account via credit card, paypal, or other means.  This is a great feature, especially for drop catching utilities like Snatcher that allow you to do instant registration when provided with your login credentials.

This has been another episode of Snatching with Sarah - thanks for watching guys!  For more drop catching information, visit www.snatcher.org

metadata.title: Royal Rumble over Forbes Domain Valuation Method
metadata.author: domainsherpa
metadata.shortDescription:
Serial entrepreneur Michael Gargiulo, CEO of VPN.com, rejoins us to discuss the ongoing success of VPN.com, the decreased cost of customer acquisition provided by an Exact Match Domain, and his novice Forbes article where he tries his hand at exact match domain valuations. He and Andrew Rosener of MediaOptions.com, the #1 global expert in domain valuation and creator of the domain industry standard’s valuation methodology, The Rosener Equation, get into a heated debate about how to value EMDs, and a Royal Rumble ensues!

Hear about the eight recent offers on VPN.com and its increasing market domination, which Gargiulo says are in large part to permanent VPN market differentiation and mechanics in marketing offered by an Exact Match Domain. Plus, Andrew Rosener makes predictions about a major shift in EMD values in the near future.

Check out www.domainsherpa.com for more info (watch the full episode here https://www.domainsherpa.com/emd-valuations/ )!

Don't forget to check us out at https://www.facebook.com/DomainSherpa
and follow us on https://www.twitter.com/DomainSherpa

Sherpas:
Andrew Rosener: https://www.twitter.com/AndrewRosener
Michael Gargiulo: https://www.linkedin.com/in/michaelvpn/

For the Best High Value Domains visit https://www.MediaOptions.com

metadata.author: domainsherpa
metadata.shortDescription:
The Whole Nine Yards - November 19, 2026

DomainSherpa Review is the flagship show on the DomainSherpa Network, where we get into the minds of successful domain name investors — who we call Sherpas — and talk about the value of domain names. By listening to the Sherpas discuss their investments, valuations, strategies, and experiences in the domain industry, we expand our knowledge and understanding so that we can become more successful domain investors ourselves.

In this episode, JT is joined by Drew, Shane, and Andrew Miller for another DomainSherpa Review. The Sherpas play The Domain Game featuring Yardley.com, MaceAI.com, UXun.com, and ByCaro.com, review upcoming NameJet auctions, and recap NamesCon, including the domain auction and the Beanstalk Challenge.

The Sherpas also get into current events and discuss how they could impact domain names and the domain industry.

In This Episode:
1️⃣ The Domain Game — Starting at 39:21.The Sherpas play The Domain Game, where they guess what certain domains were bought and sold for and then discuss the reasoning behind their valuations. Today’s domains are Yardley.com, MaceAI.com, UXun.com, and ByCaro.com. Follow along with the Sherpas, make your own guesses, and see how your domain valuations compare before the actual numbers are revealed.
2️⃣ Upcoming NameJet Domain Auctions. The Sherpas review another group of domain names coming up for auction on NameJet.com, discussing the names and sharing their thoughts on the upcoming inventory. This episode’s NameJet list includes Rebuilding.com, StationHouse.com, SnowHawk.com, and Southern.org.
3️⃣ NamesCon Recap. Fresh off NamesCon, the Sherpas recap the show and discuss some of the highlights from the event. They get into the NamesCon domain auction, the Beanstalk Challenge, and more from this year’s conference.
4️⃣ Current Events & the Domain Industry. The Sherpas also discuss some current events and how those developments could impact domain names and the broader domain industry.
5️⃣ DomainSherpa now integrates with Skiv.com (formerly Muse.ai), featuring searchable transcripts and an AI-powered video player so you can instantly jump to any topic, domain, or discussion point.
6️⃣ Watch all DomainSherpa episodes on DS.tv and stay plugged into the Sherpa Network.

0:00 - Introduction
2:57 - Grand opening and does the audience want a Sherpa swag store?
6:48 - The Sherpas recap NamesCon, the domain auction, and the Beanstalk Challenge
13:05 - They get into Bentley's, Ferrari's, and luxury cars
19:13 - More NamesCon recap and the "comedy" roast

39:21 - The Domain Game begins with a recent domain sale from Drew, Yardly.com
46:01 - Second round of the Domain Game has a sale from Miller, MaceAI.com
49:13 - JT goes over some Appraise.net valuations
49:57 - The next round of the Domain Game has a buy from Shane, UXun.com
53:54 - They go down memory lane of historic domain auctions with domains such as QR.com
56:40 - The Domain Game concludes with a listed sale, Bycaro.com and the rest of the Domain Game Appraise.net valuations
1:00:20 - #MediaOptrions sponsor break
1:00:55 - It's the #NameJetGonnaJet segment where the Sherpas review a list of domains about to come up for auction on NameJet, such as Rebuilding.com and Sourthern.org
1:11:03 - =Drew discusses why he likes StationHouse.com and SnowHawk.com and the recent battle in Portugal with Asian hornets
1:19:49 - Grand closing and more on the current state of the world and impact on domains

Watch the full interview: http://www.domainsherpa.com/andrew-rosener-300k-interview/

We all lose money when first starting out in domain name investing, because part of the process of figuring things out inevitably includes buying worthless or undesirable domain names.

The same was true for today's guest.

But instead of just buying 100 or so worthless domain names, he invested in a "domain name education" that cost him about $300,000 over three years until he realized what he was doing wrong.

Today, he runs one of the most successful domain name brokerages. Listen in as Andrew Rosener shares what he learned from his expensive "education."

metadata.title: The Future of Domains with Andrew Rosener | HANDYCON
metadata.author: SkyInclude
metadata.shortDescription:
The Future of Domains with Andrew Rosener recap

What makes a domain name valuable? What could make decentralized domain names valuable in the future? Andrew shares his "thesis" around his investments on Handshake and other decentralized domain name protocols.

About Andrew Rosener
He is the CEO at MediaOptions,  a leading Domain Broker and experts in domain name sales & acquisitions and pioneers in domain valuation

The HANDSHAKE CONFERENCE (HANDYCON) provides us the best and finest insights through experienced speakers and valuable content.

Here's a complete list of HandyCon speakers who shared their valuable knowledge and insights of the new internet: 
http://handycon.promote.hns.to/

Organizers:
Jehan Chu of Kenetic Capital
Mike Michelini of Global From Asia and SkyInclude

#handshake #handycon #decentralizedweb

Batten Down the Hatches - November 11, 2026

DomainSherpa Review is the flagship show on the DomainSherpa Network, where we get into the minds of successful domain name investors, who we call Sherpas, and talk about the value of domain names. By listening to the Sherpas discuss their investments, valuations, strategies, and experiences in the domain industry, we expand our knowledge and understanding so that we can become more successful domain investors ourselves.

IThe Sherpas play The Domain Game featuring Techno.com, Ways.io, Carbon.org, and AstroPunk.com, review upcoming NameJet auctions, catch up with Josh, and discuss NamesCon, the domain auction, and the Beanstalk Challenge.

Drew also shares some of his favorite Beanstalk Challenge projects from his perspective as one of the judges, the Sherpas briefly get into handling taxes in domains, and Mike gives an update on Notify.domains.

1️⃣ The Domain Game — 52:26. The Sherpas put their domain valuation skills to the test, guessing what domains were bought and sold for and breaking down the reasoning behind their valuations. Today’s domains are Techno.com, Ways.io, Carbon.org, and AstroPunk.com.

metadata.title: Navigating Appraised Value vs Market Value of Your Domain
metadata.author: domainsherpa
metadata.shortDescription:
At the NamesCon Europe conference in Portugal this summer, 4 of the top minds in domain name valuation discussed what factors influence domain name valuation and how to navigate appraised value versus market value.

Determining the appraised value of your assets is important as you hold your domain name assets. Separate is determining the monetization value: both in what you can draw from the held asset, and what you can expect the market to actually bear at the time of sale.

Braden Pollock moderates a panel of domain name brokers and experts: Ammar Kubba, Joe Styler, Andrew Rosener, and Morgan Linton come together to analyze variables in domain name valuation.

First, hear these experts discuss why you need to be informed about the ICA, of which Andrew Rosener says, “The only thing between you and the loss of your domain is the ICA.”

Then, they discuss:
(i) Wholesale domain prices & liquidity
(ii) Enterprise value (particularly with insights from the recent Voice.com sale)
(iii) When comps matter, and what may and may not be considered a comparable sale
(iv) The Rosener Equation and what the experts understand
(v) The importance of, and challenges of, refreshing an investment portfolio
(vi) Domain auctions and pricing variations
(vii) JT, Jonathan Tenenbaum from NameJet, jumps in to share insight on  the heuristics of domain 
        auctions and patterns the experts have seen in perceived buyer values too!
(viii) Creating an agreed upon valuation methodology

Check out www.domainsherpa.com for more info (watch the full episode here https://www.domainsherpa.com/appraised-market-value-domains/ )!

Don't forget to check us out at https://www.facebook.com/DomainSherpa
and follow us on https://www.twitter.com/DomainSherpa

Sherpas:
Andrew Rosener: https://www.twitter.com/AndrewRosener
Jonathan Tenenbaum: https://www.twitter.com/J10enbaum

For the Best High Value Domains visit https://www.MediaOptions.com
