metadata.shortDescription:
Atomic Habits - October 29, 2026

Welcome back to DomainSherpa Review, the flagship show on the DomainSherpa Network where we get into the minds of successful domain name investors — the Sherpas — and talk about the value of domain names. By listening to the Sherpas, we expand our knowledge and understanding so that we can become more successful domain investors ourselves.

In this episode, JT is joined by Drew, Shane, Andrew Miller, and Zack Gabor of Atom.com, making his DomainSherpa debut.

With Zack joining the show, the Sherpas get an inside update on Atom.com, the latest developments with its Ultra Premium Marketplace, and the broader state of domain marketplaces. They also revisit the .SI domain trend and its impact on .AI domains, play another round of The Domain Game, and review upcoming NameJet auctions.

In This Episode:
1️⃣ The Domain Game. Starting at the 52:20 mark, the Sherpas play The Domain Game, where they guess what certain domains were bought and sold for and discuss the reasoning behind their valuations. Today’s domains are Asia.net, Ojo.co, WhoDecides.com, and Qontext.com. See how the Sherpas value each name and compare their estimates with the actual purchase and sale prices.
2️⃣ Upcoming NameJet Auctions. The Sherpas review a selection of domains coming up for auction on NameJet.com and share their thoughts on the names and their potential value. Domains include GardenFlowers.com, TheLeaf.com, Fore.org, and Committee.net.
3️⃣ Atom.com & the Ultra Premium Marketplace. Zack Gabor joins DomainSherpa for the first time to give an update on Atom.com and what’s happening across the platform. The Sherpas discuss the latest developments with Atom’s Ultra Premium Marketplace and the evolving landscape for premium domain marketplaces.
4️⃣ The State of Domain Marketplaces. The conversation expands into the broader domain marketplace landscape and how the market continues to evolve. The Sherpas share their perspectives on domain marketplaces and what recent developments could mean for domain investors.
5️⃣ .SI Domains & the Impact on .AI. The Sherpas revisit the .SI domain trend and discuss what the emergence of .SI could mean for the .AI domain market. They get into the relationship between the two extensions and the potential impact of .SI on .AI domains.
6️⃣ DomainSherpa now integrates with Skiv.com (formerly Muse.ai), featuring searchable transcripts and an AI-powered video player so you can instantly jump to any topic, domain, or discussion point.
7️⃣ Watch all DomainSherpa episodes on DS.tv and stay plugged into the Sherpa Network.

0:00 - Introduction
3:30 - Grand opening and a jump down the rabbit hole of home remodeling
9:50 - Andrew Miller is introduced and Zack Gabor of Atom.com makes his DomainSherpa debut!

52:20 - The Domain Game begins with a recent purchase from Drew, Asia.net and the Sherpas get into which TLDs are underutilized
57:24 - The next round of the Domain Game with a buy from Shane, Ojo.co
100:36 - The Domain Game continues with a domain sale from Miller, WhoDecides.com
1:03:33 - The Domain Game concludes with an Atom sale revealed by Zack, Qontext.com
1:09:13 - #MediaOptions sponsor break

1:14:33 - It's the #NameJetGonnaJet segment where the Sherpas review a list of domains about to come up for auction on NameJet, such as TheLeaf.com and Fescue.com and why Shane think plant brands are valuable

1:29:02 - The Sherpas get into a debate on the .si trend and their impact on .ai domains .si discussion

metadata.shortDescription:
The Carrot and the Stick - March 19, 2026

Welcome back to DomainSherpa Review, the flagship podcast where experienced domain investors break down real deals, auction opportunities, market dynamics, and the strategies that separate average portfolios from elite ones.

In this episode titled “The Carrot and the Stick,” JT is joined by Drew, Shane, and Bar Franek for a wide-ranging discussion that goes beyond just domain valuations and diving into incentive structures, industry friction points, and the biggest mistakes domain investors continue to make.

From real-world domain comps to auction analysis, to a candid “Grind My Gears” segment calling out industry shortcomings, this episode blends tactical insight with unfiltered perspective on what’s working and what’s not working in today’s domain market.

If you’re buying, selling, or building in domains, this one hits on both the strategy and the psychology behind better outcomes.

In This Episode:
1️⃣The Domain Game – Starts at 18:17. The Sherpas break down recent domain sales and walk through how they evaluate value, brandability, and end-user potential. This week’s domains are WH.org, Karnivore.com, Ploob.com, and OldTimeCandy.com. Expect sharp takes across acronyms, brandables, and category-driven names.
2️⃣ NameJet Auction Review. The Sherpas review domains coming up for auction, such as VOSO.com, Wisemen.com, YellowParrot.com, and TheStick.com. The Sherpas evaluate positioning, buyer pools, and how these names may perform in today’s auction environment.
3️⃣ Grind My Gears – Industry Callouts. A candid segment where the Sherpas discuss domain industry participants and providers they believe could be doing a better job, while highlighting friction points and areas for improvement across the ecosystem.
4️⃣ Rick Schwartz’s Beanstalk Challenge. The Sherpas discuss Rick Schwartz’s initiative to build out select domains, exploring what it means for domain owners and how development can play a role in unlocking value.
5️⃣ The Carrot vs. The Stick. What actually drives behavior in domain deals? The Sherpas debate incentive structures and whether positive reinforcement or pressure-based tactics are more effective when negotiating and closing deals.
6️⃣ The Biggest Mistake Domainers Make. Drew shares what he believes is the most common and costly mistake domain investors make when buying and selling domains and how to avoid it.
7️⃣New Sponsor: Appraise.net. Big news — Appraise.net is now a DomainSherpa sponsor.
8️⃣ DomainSherpa now integrates with Skiv.com (formerly Muse.ai), featuring searchable transcripts and an AI-powered video player so you can instantly jump to any topic, domain, or discussion point.
9️⃣ Watch all DomainSherpa episodes on DS.tv and stay plugged into the Sherpa Network.

By listening to the Sherpas, we expand our knowledge and understanding so that we can become more successful domain investors ourselves.

(ii) They play The Domain Game, where they guess what certain domains were bought and sold for and discuss the reasons behind their evaluations. metadata.author: domainsherpa
metadata.shortDescription:
Shoot For The Moon - September 3, 2026

Welcome back to DomainSherpa Review, the flagship podcast where experienced domain investors break down real domain sales, upcoming auction opportunities, pricing strategies, and the challenges that come with buying and selling premium domain names.

In this episode titled “Shoot For The Moon,” JT is joined by Drew, Ammar, and Mike Cyger for a wide-ranging discussion on identifying which names deserve ambitious, moonshot-level pricing. The Sherpas also dig into what happens when a buyer defaults on a lease-to-own deal, recent changes to online domain appraisal tools, and some of the challenges they’ve experienced when working with escrow services.

From Attorney.org and Supa.app in The Domain Game to Tricky.com and other upcoming NameJet auctions, this episode combines real-world domain evaluations with practical conversations about pricing, transactions, and navigating the domain aftermarket.

In This Episode:
1️⃣ The Domain Game – Starts at 22:37. The Sherpas guess what domains were bought and sold for and discuss the reasoning behind their valuations. This week’s domains are Attorney.org, ForEverybody.com, Supa.app, and HealthcareX.com. The Sherpas compare their evaluations and break down the factors they consider when determining what each domain may be worth.
2️⃣ NameJet Auction Review. The Sherpas review domains about to come up for auction on NameJet, including MIHI.com, SharkFin.com, Tricky.com, and WorldWideTravel.com. They evaluate the names and discuss their potential from a domain investor’s perspective.
3️⃣ Selecting Domains for Moonshot Pricing. The Sherpas break down their approach to selecting domains for moonshot pricing and discuss the considerations that go into deciding which names warrant aiming higher.
4️⃣ What Happens When an LTO Deal Defaults? The Sherpas discuss the right approach when a buyer defaults on a lease-to-own domain deal and the considerations that come with deciding what to do next.
5️⃣ Domain Appraisal Tool Updates. The conversation turns to recent updates involving certain online domain appraisal tools.
6️⃣ Challenges With Escrow Services. The Sherpas also discuss some of the challenges that can arise when working with escrow services during domain transactions.
7️⃣ Mike’s Bainbridge Island Walk. Mike shares some thoughts from his recent walk around Bainbridge Island.
8️⃣ Sponsor: Appraise.net. Big news — Appraise.net is now a DomainSherpa sponsor.
9️⃣ DomainSherpa now integrates with Skiv.com (formerly Muse.ai), featuring searchable transcripts and an AI-powered video player so you can instantly jump to any topic, domain, or discussion point.
🔟 Watch all DomainSherpa episodes on DS.tv and stay plugged into the Sherpa Network.

3:33 - Gran opening and some high fashion advice from the Sherpas
10:30 - Ammar gives his pickleball update and Mike breaks down his 41 mile walk around Bainbridge Island
16:09 - The Sherpas discuss MediaOptions recent domain submission request

27:31 - Drew shares a past memory of Rob Monster
30:52 - Second round of the Domain Game has a buy from Ammar, ForEverybody.com and leads to a discussion of best practices when LTO deals default
40:52 - Appraise.net valuations of some domain names and updates on domain appraisal tools, such as GoDaddy
52:42 - The Domain Game continues with a sale from Cyger on a  domain name he bought from his last appearance, Supa.app
59:07 - More appraise.net valuations and challenges with Escrow services
1:07:24 - The Domain Game concludes with tie breaker and buy from Drew, HealthcareX.com
1:11:30 - The Sherpas dig into how to select domains for moonshot pricing
SMILES 1:19:16

1:33:33 - Drew explains why he likes the CVCV domain names and WorldWideTravel.com

metadata.title: GoDaddy’s Aftermarket Approach: Normalizing Premium Domain Acquisitions
metadata.author: domainsherpa
metadata.shortDescription:
GoDaddy created a new position, Senior Premium Domain Name Consultant, with Jebidiah Burnett filling the consultative sales role with his tremendous expertise. GoDaddy has amassed a significant premium domain name portfolio over the past years via several valuable portfolio acquisitions, and this is their next strategic step. Given the rising tide of the domain industry and the tipping point we’ve been discussing in end user education on domain name values, this is a statement for the entire ecosystem.

With Andrew Rosener joining us, we also discuss insights on the market in general and trends & feedback these two brokers are receiving from their daily interactions with premium domain buyers.

If you’re looking for insights into the domain industry or premium domain acquisition trends by end users, enjoy the show!

Check out www.domainsherpa.com for more info (watch the full episode here https://www.domainsherpa.com/premium-acquisitions/ )!
Don't forget to check us out at https://www.facebook.com/DomainSherpa
and follow us on https://www.twitter.com/DomainSherpa

Sherpas:
Andrew Rosener: https://www.twitter.com/AndrewRosener
Jebidiah Burnett: https://www.twitter.com/DonutsInc

For the Best High Value Domains visit https://www.MediaOptions.com

metadata.author: domainsherpa
metadata.shortDescription:
Watch the full show: http://www.domainsherpa.com/andrew-rosener-dnx-interview/ ‎

In real estate, the stock market or domain name investing, it's an oft-stated business rule that you make your money on the buy, not the sell.

But how do you make sure you're value investing like Warren Buffett in the domain name industry? What do top domain name brokers look for when buying domain names for their own personal investment portfolio?

Today's interview answers those questions and more. Warning: this is a long show, but it's well worth your time as there are nuggets of gold around finding generic premium domains, contacting hard-to-locate registrants, making offers and a new reverse auction sales platform that's offering some great buying opportunities. Real buy and sell information, including pricing, is discussed.

Bonus: The real story behind the rumored mid-six figure domain name sale of Internet.org to Mark Zuckerberg/Facebook and how today's guest was involved.

metadata.title: Down the Domain & Crypto Rabbit Hole – with Bitcoin Developer Jimmy Song
metadata.author: domainsherpa
metadata.shortDescription:
Go down the domain & crypto rabbit hole with Bitcoin developer & evangelist, Jimmy Song! 

In followup to our Charlie Shrem interview, we’re continuing our examination of the unique overlap of crypto and domains. Jimmy is joined by Andrew Rosener, global expert in the domain name market and domain valuations. We explore every rabbit hole :
(i) Living an Antifragile Life
(ii) Is the domain DNS system a potential Achilles heel for crypto’s transactional security?
(iii) How Jimmy’s Bitcoin quote applies to domain name values: “Credible long-term scarcity is why 
       people buy Bitcoin. In other words, people want Bitcoins because they see it as a good store of 
       value.”
(iv) Jimmy’s famous “magical blockchain dust” comment: Jimmy and Andrew’s thoughts on the 3-5 
       year trajectory of end-users’ disconnect in understanding crypto and domain name values
(v) The crypto industry’s domain acquisitions: from .io to .com domain names
(vi) Finally, a mega rabbit hole about how many crypto enthusiasts apply the antifragility lifestyle to 
       their dietary habits

Investors and entrepreneurs who are curious about- or preparing for- the future will benefit from today’s show!

Check out www.domainsherpa.com for more info (watch the full episode here https://www.domainsherpa.com/bitcoin-jimmy-song/ )

Don't forget to check us out at https://www.facebook.com/DomainSherpa
and follow us on https://www.twitter.com/DomainSherpa

Sherpas:
Andrew Rosener: https://www.twitter.com/AndrewRosener
Jimmy Song: https://www.twitter.com/jimmysong

For the Best High Value Domains visit https://www.MediaOptions.com

metadata.title: 3 Things Brokers Look for Before Taking On a Domain for Outbound
metadata.author: SawSells
metadata.shortDescription:
Would a top domain broker take these two AI and robotics domains?

Jeff Gabriel reviews CogRL and RobotWRLD live, checking search demand, potential buyers, and pricing to decide whether they're a fit for Saw.com's outbound brokerage.

00:00 Intro
00:16 What Makes a Domain Worth Brokering
00:45 First Look: CogRL and RobotWRLD
01:46 Researching CogRL's Search Demand
03:49 Why a Domain Needs Obvious Buyers
04:14 Digging Into RobotWRLD
05:02 Typos, Brand Protection and the Whoop Exception
06:05 The 4 Questions Every Broker Asks
07:17 The Verdict

A domain owner asked Saw.com to sell two names through our premium outbound brokerage service. Before taking on any name, Jeff looks for one thing: a clear target he can call and tell, with conviction, that they need this domain for their business. In this video he walks through his real process, from keyword research and domain history to checking who else owns the name across other extensions, and explains why a $200,000 asking price changes the conversation.

Want Jeff's take on your domain? Tag us and it could be featured in a future video.

Saw.com is a domain brokerage behind $565M+ in premium domain sales, founded by Jeff Gabriel. Buy, sell, or appraise at https://saw.com

About Jeffrey M. Gabriel
Jeffrey is the founder of Saw.com, a domain brokerage specializing in domain acquisition, sales, and appraisals. With over 15 years of experience, Jeffrey has closed some of the most notable multimillion dollar domain sales in history, including Ai.com, Sex.com, and Poker.org. He is also a Guinness World Record holder and a frequent speaker and writer on domain related topics.

Follow Saw.com
Website: https://saw.com
LinkedIn: https://linkedin.com/company/saw-com
X (Twitter): https://x.com/sawsells
Facebook: https://facebook.com/sawcom

Subscribe for more conversations from inside the domain industry.

metadata.title: Turn Atom’s Top-Selling Keywords into a Daily Domain Deal Flow
metadata.author: GoDaddy Domain Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Most domain investors see a great data tweet, hit like, and scroll on.
In this video, I walk you step-by-step through how to take Atom’s 2025 top-selling root keywords and turn them into a practical, daily workflow for finding better domain opportunities!

What you’ll learn in this video:
00:00 – Intro: From data tweet to action plan
01:05 – Grabbing Atom’s 2025 top-selling keywords
02:00 – Using ChatGPT (or simple text tools) to format keyword lists
03:20 – Setting up targeted filters on ExpiredDomains.net
05:15 – Limiting to brandable, 2-word .coms without hyphens or numbers
06:10 – Saving custom searches for ongoing use
07:30 – Using “Only New Domains” so you never re-scan the same list
09:00 – How to adapt this process for other marketplaces and TLDs
10:30 – Practical tips to evaluate whether the brand + keyword combo makes sense

Instead of treating keyword sales charts as trivia, this process helps you turn them into a repeatable sourcing system. Tomorrow, next week, and next month you can come back and see only the new names that match the exact type of inventory that sells.

Resources mentioned
• Atom.com (formerly Squadhelp) tweet with 2025 top-selling root keywords https://x.com/darpanmunjal/status/2005632453080392174?s=20
• ExpiredDomains.net – Saved searches and “Only New Domains”
• Adaptable for any platform you purchase names. 

Learn more at Domain Academy
At Domain Academy, we focus on practical, repeatable methods for building a profitable portfolio:
• Step-by-step classes on domain investing, portfolio strategy, and outbound
• Proprietary tools and workflows for daily domain research
• Real-world training on what actually sells and why

Explore our training and tools:
https://www.domainacademy.com
If you are actively investing in domains and want better economics on your registrations and renewals, consider Domain Discount Club Pro:
https://www.godaddy.com/domains/discount-domain-club?utm_source=Domain-Academy&utm_medium=DDC-link&utm_campaign=Domain_Academy_DDC

Stay connected:
Subscribe on YouTube for more deep-dive, hands-on domain investing tutorials.
Follow us on X: https://x.com/dnacademy
Connect with me on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/joestyler/
Visit Domain Academy: https://www.domainacademy.com

If you use this workflow and discover a domain you’re excited about, let me know in the comments. Share what you found (no need to post it publicly if you’re not ready) and how the method is working for you.
And if you found this helpful, please like, subscribe, and share this video with other investors who want more structured, data-driven ways to find names every day.

Remember to always do your own research and that these videos are provided for educational and informational purposes only and do not constitute investment or financial advice. Always do your own research.

metadata.title: Lessons About UDRP v. ACPA from the Debevoise Cybersquatting Case
metadata.author: GigaLaw - Doug Isenberg
metadata.shortDescription:
The Uniform Domain Name Dispute Resolution Policy (UDRP) may be the best and most popular way for trademark owners to fight cybersquatters – but it's not the only option. In fact, a domain name dispute filed by Debevoise & Plimpton, a large law firm, on its own behalf provides a good lesson about the pros and cons of going to court instead of filing a UDRP complaint.

In this video, I discuss what happened in the Debevoise case; why law firms are being targeted by cybersquatters; and why a preliminary injunction in a case under the Anti-Cybersquatting Consumer Protection Act (ACPA) -- which is what Debevoise chose to do here -- is not always the better option for every trademark when compared with the additional benefits of filing a UDRP complaint.

Resources:

​​- GigaLaw website: https://giga.law/

​- Domain Name Disputes: A Masterclass: https://giga.law/masterclass

- GigaLaw's Domain Dispute Digest: https://giga.law/digest

- About Doug Isenberg: https://giga.law/about-doug-isenberg

Disclaimer: This video is for general informational purposes only, provides only a summary of specific issues, and is not intended to be and should not be relied upon as legal advice regarding any specific situation. This video is not intended to create, and does not constitute, an attorney-client relationship. Viewers should consult with legal counsel to determine how laws, policies or decisions and other topics discussed in this video apply to the viewers' specific circumstances. This video may be considered attorney advertising under court rules of certain jurisdictions. Copyright © 2022 Douglas M. Isenberg

found itself to be the victim of a cyber

so while the firm uses the domain name

using the domain names debbo

a magistrate judge's report in a lawsuit
filed by double voice one of the domain
names was being used in connection with
a landing page filled with ads for Legal
Services
while the other domain name was used to
send phishing emails imitating a partner
at the firm and not surprisingly one of
the emails included in the complaint was
riddled with typos although perhaps they
were easy to overlook
unfortunately as I discussed in a video
earlier this year law firms are not
immune from being the targets of cyber
squatters and in fact I've seen an
increasing number of udrp complaints
filed by law firms on their own behalf
sometimes in cases in which the disputed
domain names were being used to
impersonate the firms as part of an
effort to solicit payment for falsified
invoices these so-called business email
compromise scams are becoming quite
popular and I have personally filed nine
udrp complaints that fit this scenario
just in the past two weeks
but in the devil boy's case the law firm
did not file a udrp complaint and
instead it chose to file a lawsuit in
U.S District Court for the eastern
district of Virginia under the acpa
which is the anti-cyber squatting
consumer protection act
the acpa was enacted in 1999 which is
the very same year that the first udrp
complaint was filed which means that
both legal tools the acpa and the udrp
have been available to trademark owners
for about the same amount of time
but while the udrp has become the weapon
of choice with tens of thousands of
decisions filed
acpa complaints remain relatively rare
and that's because the udrp was designed
to be a quicker and less expensive
alternative to litigation but the udrp
is not without some limitations and one
of those limitations is that unlike
disputes filed in court the udrp does
not offer a trademark owner the ability
to obtain injunctive relief that's an
interim legal ruling before the case is
fully resolved and I suspect that's why
Debo voice chose to file a complaint in
court under the acpa rather than under
the udrp
and on the one hand the law firm's
decision seems to make a lot of sense
and and by the way I know the deba voice
attorney who filed the complaint he's a
leading voice in this area of the law
and we serve together as panelists at

metadata.title: Check the USPTO Before you Brand your Business or Product
metadata.author: Carter Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
Arizona social media and trademark attorney explains the importance of checking the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s trademark database before your select a name for your business or product, or roll out a marketing campaign. If it’s too similar to someone in your industry who has registered their trademark, they can force you to rebrand.

USPTO website: http://www.uspto.gov/

More helpful links:
What’s a Trademark and Why You Should Register Yours: http://bit.ly/1o4tuLg
The Risk of Not Registering your Trademark: http://bit.ly/JhY6jB 
How to Register a Trademark with the USPTO: http://bit.ly/1g2yhaA  

You can see all the ways to contact and connect with Ruth Carter on the Carter Law Firm website:  http://carterlawaz.com/contact/. 

Disclaimer: This video does not constitute legal advice. Watching this video does not create an attorney-client relationship with any viewer. If you need personalized legal advice, hire an attorney

metadata.title: Domain Dispute Masterclass (#5): What type of trademark is required to file a UDRP complaint?
metadata.author: GigaLaw - Doug Isenberg
metadata.shortDescription:
Attorney Doug Isenberg of GigaLaw discusses the first part of the UDRP's three-part test, which requires a complainant to prove that the domain name at issue is identical or confusingly similar to a trademark or service mark in which it has rights. As Doug explains, this requirement actually consists of two parts: First, the complainant must have rights in a trademark. And second, the domain name in dispute must be identical or confusingly similar to that trademark. This video focuses just on the first part: trademark rights.

GigaLaw website: https://giga.law/

About Doug Isenberg: https://giga.law/about-doug-isenberg

0:00 - Introduction
1:01 - First part of UDRP's three-part test
1:41 - Where trademark rights exist
2:47 - U.S. state trademark registrations
3:32 - When trademark rights arose
4:24 - Registered versus common law trademarks
5:49 - Evidence of common law trademarks
7:13 - To learn more

Want to improve your website’s SEO and clean up harmful backlinks? In this video, I show you how to perform a backlink audit with Ubersuggest, so you can analyze your backlink profile, identify toxic links, and boost your search rankings.

📌 What You’ll Learn:

How to check all backlinks pointing to your website

How to identify low-quality or harmful backlinks

Step-by-step process for auditing and improving your backlink profile

Tips to leverage backlinks for higher SEO performance

Whether you’re a blogger, marketer, or business owner, this tutorial helps you protect and strengthen your website’s SEO with a thorough backlink audit.

✅ Start auditing your backlinks with Ubersuggest today and improve your search rankings!

segments.text: In today's video, I'm going to teach you
how to do a backlink audit with Uber
Suggest. Achieving a successful backlink
audit might seem daunting, but with the
right tools and understanding, you can
master it easily. To start off, we need
to visit the Uber Suggest tool on the
Neil Patel website. Make sure you're
logged into Uber Suggest to access all
the necessary features. If you're not
already familiar, Uber Suggest offers a
comprehensive suite of SEO tools that
can help you thoroughly analyze your
backlink profile.
Once you're logged in, the next step is
to enter your website URL into the
search bar and hit that search button.
This action will initiate a deep dive
into your website's backlink profile,
which is crucial for gaining insights
into how other websites link back to
yours. Now, navigate to the left menu
and click on backlinks. This can be
found under either the SEO explorer or
traffic analyzer section. Clicking here
will bring up a detailed report
showcasing all the domains that are
currently linking to your site. It's an
essential feature because it reveals
important metrics such as the referring
domains, which are essentially the
websites linking back to you. In
addition to referring domains, you'll
also see domain authority and page
authority scores. These scores give you
a sense of how strong and influential a
website is. A higher domain authority
suggests that the domain is likely more
credible, while page authority focuses
on the strength of individual pages.
You'll also want to pay attention to the
anchor text, which is crucial for
understanding the context in which the
links point to your site. Plus, you'll
see whether these are do follow or no
follow links. Do follow links pass on
SEO benefits, which is why they're
typically more desirable.

includes no follow links can also be
beneficial. The final and crucial step
of your audit is to review the quality
of these links. Identify which links are
beneficial, often coming from high
authority and relevant websites to your
niche. These are the types of links you
want as they give a good boost to your
SEO rankings. But beware of bad links
which often come from spammy or
irrelevant sites and could harm your SEO
health. If you find any of these, it's
advisable to consider disavowing them to
protect your site's ranking. And that's
it. With these steps, you now know how
to perform a thorough backlink audit
using Uber Suggest. Regular audits like
this help maintain your website's SEO
health and ensure that you're always in
the best possible standing with search
engines. Happy analyzing.

OpenSEO’s backlink checker will show you the total number of backlinks for a domain, referring domains, referring pages, rank, backlink spam score, and broken back links.

metadata.title: Backlinks from Expired Domains: The Safe Way (and the Trap Most SEOs Fall Into)
metadata.author: SERPSUPPORT
metadata.shortDescription:
Backlinks from expired domains look like the best shortcut in SEO. A dead site still has years of links, and once the domain drops, anyone can buy it. But in 2026, buying expired domains just for their links is one of the fastest ways to waste money or run into Google's spam policies. In this video we show how expired domain backlinks really work, which tactics are risky, and the one approach that earns safe links that keep their value for years.
 
If you run an affiliate site, a local business, a SaaS tool or an SEO agency, this is the expired domain link building guide to watch before you spend a cent at a domain auction.
 
⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 Years of backlinks, up for grabs
0:20 Backlinks from expired domains explained
0:28 What is an expired domain? The domain lifecycle
1:07 Why old backlinks still matter
1:37 Three ways to use expired domains
2:01 Play 1: 301 redirect an expired domain
2:44 Play 2: Rebuild it, PBNs and Google's policy
3:24 Play 3: Use the dead domain as a map
3:54 How to find expired domains in your niche
4:23 How to vet an expired domain
4:52 Outreach that earns the link
5:22 When buying a domain is legit
5:53 Recap
6:15 How SERPsupport works
6:54 Get started
 
🔎 IN THIS VIDEO
• What an expired domain is, and what happens before it drops: grace period, redemption, pending delete, auctions and backorders
• Why backlinks from expired domains keep their value long after the site is gone
• The three common plays: 301 redirects, rebuilding the site as a private blog network (PBN), and broken link building
• Why a 301 redirect from an unrelated domain rarely works now, and when a redirect still makes sense
• What Google's expired domain abuse spam policy, added in March 2024, means for SEOs and link buyers
• How to use a dead domain as a map to find sites that already want to link to a page like yours
• How to find expired domains with ExpiredDomains.net, Ahrefs, Semrush or Majestic
• How to vet a domain: Wayback Machine history, anchor text red flags like casino, pharma or foreign spam, live and indexed linking sites, and the top linked pages
• A short, honest outreach email that site owners actually reply to
• When buying an expired domain is a smart business move, and when it is the exact pattern Google warns about
 
📌 THE SHORT VERSION
Expired domains still carry backlinks, and that is real value. How you use them is what counts.
 
1. Redirect: point an unrelated expired domain at your site and the old signals are often just ignored. You pay for the domain and get little back, or you inherit spammy links. It only makes sense if the old site had the same topic and you truly carry on what it did.
 
2. Rebuild: fill an old domain with cheap content to link to your money pages, and you are in expired domain abuse territory. Add Google's rules on link schemes, and a PBN can put both the network and the sites it links to at risk.
 
3. Map: study the dead domain instead of buying it. Every expired site in your niche left behind a list of sites that linked to it because it was useful. Those links are now broken. Make a better, updated page on the same topic, reach out with a short, helpful note, and earn editorial links that nobody paid for and nothing hides.

segments.text: Hi, Alex here, founder of SER Support.
Want to build links the natural way?
Connect directly with real website
owners in your niche. Sign up for free
at serupport.com.
Now, let's go back to the video.
Somewhere right now, a website with
years of backlinks is about to
disappear. The owner forgot to renew it.
In a few weeks, anyone can register that
domain and every link pointing at it up
for grabs. That sounds like a shortcut
to better rankings. Sometimes it is.
Often it's a trap.
So, let's break down how backlinks from
expired domains really work and how to
use them without getting burned.
First, a simple definition. An expired
domain is a domain name whose
registration was not renewed, but it
doesn't vanish overnight. For a dot,
there's usually a grace period where the
old owner can still renew, often up to
45 days depending on the registar. Then
comes a 30-day redemption period. Then 5
days of pending delete, and then the
domain drops and it's back on the open
market. Many valuable names never make
it that far. Registars send them to
auction or backorder services catch them
the second they drop.
So why do SEOs care so much? Because
when a website dies, its back links
usually don't. A local newspaper that
linked to it 5 years ago still links to
it today. A university resource page
still points there. So does a popular
blog. Those links now lead to an error
page or to nothing at all. The authority
is still sitting there attached to a
domain that nobody owns. That's the
opportunity. The real question is what
you do with it. There are three common
ways people use expired domains for
links. One, redirect the whole domain to
their own site. Two, rebuild the old
site and use it to link out. and three,
use the dead domain as a map to find
links you can earn for yourself. The
first two are where most people get into
trouble. The third is where the real
lasting value is.
Let's start with redirects. The idea is
simple. Buy the expired domain, add a
301 redirect, and hope its link equity
flows into your site. Years ago, this
worked surprisingly well. Today, Google
is much better at spotting it. When a
domain changes hands and suddenly points
somewhere unrelated, the old signals can
simply be ignored. You pay for the
domain and you get nothing. Or worse,
you inherit spammy links you never
wanted. If the old site covered the
exact same topic and you're genuinely
continuing what it offered, a redirect
can make sense. If it was a bakery and
you sell software, it doesn't. The
second play is rebuilding. People
restore the old site, fill it with cheap
content, and drop links to their money
pages. Stack enough of these together,
and you have a private blog network.
Here's the problem. In March 2024,
Google added expired domain abuse to its
spam policies. It describes buying
expired domains and repurposing them
mainly to manipulate search rankings
with low value content. Combine that
with Google's long-standing rules on
link schemes, and you have a strategy
that can wipe out not just the network,
but the sites it links to.
Which brings us to the third play. And
honestly, it's the smartest one. Instead
of buying the domain, you study it.
Every expired site in your niche left
behind a list of websites that once
linked to it. Those site owners chose to
link there because the resource was
useful. Now their link is broken. That's
a bad experience for their readers. Most
of them would happily fix it if someone
handed them a good replacement. That
someone can be you. Here's how to find
them. Start with a tool like expired
domains.net and filter by keywords in
your niche. You can also use a backlink
tool like ahrefs, simrush or majestic.
Look at the broken outgoing links on

metadata.author: Edward Sturm
metadata.shortDescription:
E985: A lot of people say exact match domains stopped working years ago. In this episode, we take a closer look at whether that’s actually true.

SEO veteran David Quaid joins the show to break down how exact match domains (EMDs) still play a role in modern search strategies. We discuss when they work, when they don’t, and why many companies underestimate the value of owning keyword-focused domains.

The conversation covers real-world use cases, practical tactics, and some of the risks involved. We also explore how EMDs fit into a broader SEO strategy that includes branded domains, satellite sites, and reputation management.

We also go beyond EMDs and talk about several current debates in search, including automated content, generative engine optimization (GEO), and how AI systems choose which sources to cite.

Topics covered:
- Whether exact match domains still provide a ranking advantage in modern SEO
- Why Google reduced the power of EMDs but didn’t eliminate it
- How companies use satellite domains to control more results on page one
- The difference between building a brand domain and using keyword-focused domains
- When exact match domains outperform branded domains
- How SEOs use EMDs to compete against large companies with stronger authority
- Why controlling multiple search results can matter for reputation management
- Strategies for linking between a main site and satellite domains
- The role of topical authority and anchor text when ranking EMDs
- When exact match domains start to look spammy
- The cost and effort required to maintain multiple domains
- How automated SEO systems are being used to build and maintain satellite sites
- Whether machine-scale content is actually detectable by search engines
- Why some companies run EMD projects anonymously
- The relationship between SEO and generative engine optimization (GEO)
- Why many claims about GEO being completely different from SEO are misleading
- How AI systems decide which sources to cite
- Why self-promotional listicles may be losing effectiveness
- A technical discussion about Cloudflare, AI crawlers, and visibility in LLM citations

David also shares examples from past projects, including competing against major companies in highly competitive search markets and using EMDs to gain visibility where a branded domain could not.

If you’re interested in practical SEO strategies, search experimentation, and the evolving relationship between search engines and AI systems, this episode covers a lot of ground.

metadata.shortDescription:
Shoot your Moonshot - October 1, 2026

Welcome back to DomainSherpa Review, the flagship podcast where experienced domain investors break down real domain acquisitions and sales, live auction opportunities, valuations, and the strategies shaping today’s domain market.

In this episode titled “Shoot Your Moonshot,” JT is joined by Drew, Ammar, and special guest James Booth for a wide-ranging discussion covering .AI domains, the growing hype around .SI domains and Super Intelligence, premium domain valuations, and the ongoing auction for Inside.com.

With James on the show, the Sherpas dig into his approach to .AI domains, his strategies for the extension, and where he thinks the market could be headed.

In This Episode:
1️⃣ The Domain Game – Starts at 39:18. The Sherpas guess what several domains were bought and sold for and break down the reasoning behind their valuations. This week’s domains are Vin.ai, PetX.com, Thirty.com, and YogaVerse.com. The discussion gets into acquisition prices, potential end users, valuation, positioning, and how the Sherpas think about pricing domains for the right buyer.
2️⃣ NameJet Auction Review. The Sherpas debate domains coming up for auction at NameJet including Commissary.com, Expressionist.com, and HigherEducation.org. The Sherpas discuss the names, their potential value, and how they would approach them as domain investors.
3️⃣ James Booth on .AI Domains. With James Booth joining the show, the Sherpas dive into the .AI domain market and discuss his strategies and predictions for the extension. They explore the current .AI landscape and how James approaches buying, valuing, and positioning these domains.
4️⃣ Super Intelligence & the .SI Domain Hype. The conversation shifts to Super Intelligence and the growing attention around .SI domains. The Sherpas discuss the current hype surrounding the extension and what is driving interest in .SI as Super Intelligence becomes a bigger part of the conversation.
5️⃣ The Inside.com Auction. The Sherpas also discuss the ongoing auction for Inside.com, breaking down the premium domain and the auction surrounding it.
6️⃣ DomainSherpa now integrates with Skiv.com (formerly Muse.ai), featuring searchable transcripts and an AI-powered video player so you can instantly jump to any topic, domain, or discussion point.
7️⃣ Watch all DomainSherpa episodes on DS.tv and stay plugged into the Sherpa Network.

0:00 - Introduction
3:24 - Grand opening and Ammar and James Booth are introduced
7:44 - The Sherpas breakdown the recent surge in .si domain registrations after President Trump touted Super Intelligence
16:00 - They go down memory lane and discuss the history of .ai and Artificial Intelligence
20:52 - James gives his insight on the current .ai market
24:14 - The Sherpas discuss Elon Musk's history with X.ai
32:18 - JT brings up the point that .si can make people think of Sports Illustrated instead of Super intelligence 
39:18 - The Domain Game begins with a recent domain purchase from Drew, VIN.ai and they debate more on the .ai domain market
50:25 - JT gives the Appraise.net valuation and the Sherpas go down the rabbit hole of vacationing in the Maldives
55:47 - Second round of the Domain Game with a domain sale from Ammar, PetX.com
1:01:30 - They go over the Appraise.net valuation
1:04:21 - Domain Game round three has a buy from James, Thirty.com and the Sherpas get into his highest priced domain and what he considers his best names.  Plus the Appraise.net valuation
1:10:20 - They discuss the current domain auction for Inside.com and the gTLD .fart
1:14:36 - The Domain Game concludes with another sale from Ammar, YogaVerse.com
1:17:23 - #MediaOptions sponsor break
1:17?:56 - They discuss more about the Inside.com auction
1:22:36 - It's the #NameJetGonnaJet segment where the Sherpas review a list of domains about to come up for auction on NameJet, such as HigherEducation.org, GetGuns.com, and Orcha.net
1:29:28 - More NameJet domains such as RedHawks.com and SPNR.com are discussed

metadata.title: Exact Match Domain Hack for AI Visibility (0 to $7M in 10 days)
metadata.author: LLMrefs AI SEO
metadata.shortDescription:
A viral post on X showed a brand-new site, bestaidatalabs.com, ranking #1 on Google within 10 days. The company it recommends, zeton.ai, was the first name in Google's AI Overview.

Exact match domains really do work for AI visibility. AI answers are built from search results, and people ask AI long, specific questions. A site that matches the question word for word, with nobody else competing for it, becomes the obvious source for the AI to cite.

We looked at how this one was built:
→ 22 near-identical "Zeton Reference" sites, all recommending one company
→ 19 domains registered within 35 seconds
→ Every site scores DR 27 on Ahrefs' current Domain Rating, and 0 on the new DR4
→ Google's spam policy lists this exact setup as "doorway abuse", and since May 2026 that policy covers AI Overviews too

The exact match is the lesson. The network is the risk.

📖 Full breakdown: https://llmrefs.com/blog
📊 Track your brand's visibility in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Overviews: https://llmrefs.com

Original post by @margatix: https://x.com/margatix/status/2119089991217262884

Subscribe: https://www.youtube.com/domainsherpa                                                
Full Episode: https://youtu.be/35YUAM-dUn0?si=BBB-fwSbEFuC2Hpf

In this highlight reel episode of the DomainSherpa Review, JT is joined by Drew, Ammar, and James Booth for a discussion covering the explosive rise of .AI domains, the emerging interest in .SI, premium domain valuation, AI startup branding, and why exact-match .COMs remain the ultimate long-term digital asset.

The Sherpas play the Domain Game featuring Vin.ai, PetX.com, and several standout premium sales, debating AI domain pricing, category-defining brands, long-term investment strategy, and how experienced investors evaluate opportunities across both .AI and .COM. They also discuss why premium one-word domains continue appreciating while AI-powered valuation tools are raising seller expectations across the market.

The panel also reviews upcoming NameJet auctions including Commissary.com, Expressionist.com, Orca.net, and GeneTechnology.com before diving into AI startup adoption, the future of .SI domains, venture-backed branding, and why controlling your exact-match .COM becomes even more valuable as AI makes products easier to build but brands harder to replace. 

As AI lowers the barrier to building products, premium brands, and the domains behind them, become the last true competitive moat. 


👇 Scroll down for full timestamps, insights, and Sherpa wisdom!

🧠 In This Episode, You'll Learn:
- Why .AI domains continue outperforming expectations in the startup market
- Whether .SI domains have the potential to follow a similar adoption curve
- How premium domain valuations are evolving in the AI era
- Why venture-backed startups increasingly prioritize exact-match brands
- How AI may ultimately make premium .COM domains even more valuable

metadata.title: Domain Escrow Explained: How to Sell Safely
metadata.author: Domains No Broker
metadata.shortDescription:
Selling a domain name can involve a significant amount of money, so it is important to understand how escrow works before transferring ownership to a buyer.

In this Domains No Broker tutorial, you’ll learn how domain escrow helps protect both buyers and sellers during a domain transaction. We’ll explain how the process works, why payment should be verified, and why you should follow the agreed transaction procedure before transferring your domain.

In this video, you’ll learn:

• What domain escrow is and how it works
• Why escrow can help reduce transaction risks
• How buyers and sellers can protect themselves against fraud
• What to verify before transferring a domain name
• Why you should follow the agreed payment and transfer process

Important: Use a reputable escrow provider and verify the transaction independently. Never transfer a domain based only on a payment screenshot or an unverified promise of payment. Check the provider’s terms and follow its approved instructions.

Learn more about direct domain buying and selling at:
https://domainsnobroker.com

Subscribe for practical videos about domain valuation, listing strategy, negotiation, secure payments, transfers, and portfolio management.

#DomainNames #DomainInvesting #DomainsNoBroker

metadata.title: Finalizing a Domain Name Purchase with Escrow
metadata.author: Name Experts
metadata.shortDescription:
Finalizing a domain name purchase is best done with escrow. 

Using an escrow service ensures the domain is transferred into the buyer's registrar before any money changes hands.

Plus, with services like escrow.com the language in their terms are usually an adequate replacement of a contract.

This gives peace of mind to both buyer and seller when a domain purchase is being finalized.

Visit https://nameexperts.com/2019/10/24/why-use-domain-brokering-buy-service/ to learn more.

domains to see the domains currently

title. In this example, we will use

2. These templates determine how your
domain page will appear. Now, we will
enter the domain name, youtube.com.sg.

select the form type. In this example,
we will choose both inside tab. This

emails, bidder confirmation emails, and

section allows you to customize the
messages shown to users after submitting
forms. Here you can configure the
escrow.com integration. You can also
customize the payment form and purchase
invitation notifications.

JavaScript for additional customization.
You can manage backups and activate your
plug-in license here. Finally, inside
the tools menu, you will find import and
export options. This allows you to
easily migrate domains, offers, and
plug-in configurations.

plug-in provides everything you need to
showcase, manage, and securely sell your

layouts, offer management, and
escrow.com integration, it gives domain
investors a complete solution for
selling domains online. If you found
this tutorial helpful, feel free to
explore the plug-in and start listing
your domains today. Thanks for watching.

metadata.shortDescription:
Reversion to the Mean - March 12, 2026

As we say on DomainSherpa , all roads lead to domains. In this episode of Sherpa Shorts, JT and Drew are joined by Sofia Canala and special guest Tony Yan, Director of Operations at Escrow.com, making his DomainSherpa debut.

This episode takes a deep dive into the Escrow.com Domain Investment Index for Q4 2025, one of the most important data snapshots of the domain aftermarket. The Sherpas unpack what the numbers reveal about the current state of the domain market,  including trends around .com, .ai, and how domain transactions are evolving as new technologies and startup demand reshape the landscape.

Whether you’re a domain investor, startup founder, or digital asset enthusiast, this episode breaks down how to interpret market data and what signals actually matter when evaluating the direction of the domain industry.

In This Episode:
1️⃣ Escrow.com Q4 2025 Domain Investment Index. The Sherpas analyze the latest report from Escrow.com and discuss what the data shows about the health of the domain market. Key themes include the transaction trends across .com and .ai domains andwhat the latest numbers reveal about investor behavior.  Plus, how these trends compare to previous reports and market cycles.
2️⃣ Mean vs. Median. What’s the Right Metric?A key part of the discussion centers around how domain data should actually be measured. The Sherpas explore why median vs. mean matters when interpreting domain sales data and which metric better reflects the real state of the market.  Plus, how investors and analysts should think about the numbers inside industry reports.
3️⃣ Geographic Domain Trends. The conversation also explores geographic insights revealed by Escrow.com’s data. The Sherpas discuss regional activity patterns in domain transactions and what Escrow is seeing globally on their platform.  They also get into how location can influence buyer demand and domain investment trends.
4️⃣ Inside Escrow.com Operations. Tony Yan shares insight into his role as Director of Operations at Escrow.com, discussing how the company operates behind the scenes and how the platform continues to scale to support the domain industry. The Sherpas talk about Tony’s work helping manage and improve Escrow’s operational systems, the importance of trusted escrow infrastructure for domain transactions, and Escrow.com’s role in supporting the global domain aftermarket.
5️⃣ DomainSherpa now integrates with Skiv.com, enabling searchable transcripts and an AI-powered video player so viewers can instantly jump to any topic, phrase, or domain mentioned in the episode.
6️⃣ You can also watch all DomainSherpa episodes on our YouTube channel at DS.tv.

0:00 - Introduction
2:31 - Grand opening and Sherpa introductions
6:04 - Tony Yan from Escrow is introduced, including his new role at the company
8:15 - The Sherpas start to dig into the 2025 Q4 Domain Investment Index report
11:30 - The difference between medium vs mean
14:52 - The Sherpas dive further into the report
26:55 -  Tony explains why Escrow uses mean over medium with .ai domains
28:02 - How can Escrow normalize the data and the Sherpas cover the .ai domain trend
35:54 - The Sherpas don't all agree on the .ai boom being reported in the index
49:38 - They discuss the Chinese market cycle and other geographical trends
59:09 - Tony and the crew explains why Escrow doesn't accept crypto payments
1:09:32 - A discussion on different category of 4-L .com domains and how it effects the data in the report
1:15:25 - #MediaOptions sponsor break
1:16:02 - More on Tony's new role at Escrow and how the Sherpas think the level of support and competency has fallen at Escrow recenlty
1:21:48 - Seller side trust with cure periods within Escrow's platform are talked about.
1:30:34 - Drew goes over some KYC issues at Escrow and Tony explains the benefits of Escrow's licenses, KYC, and insurance levels on backend
1:41:29 - Escrow 2.0 platform launch is announced

segments.text: ICANN has launched a tool called the
Name Collision Observatory or NCO.
This is a web-based tool that helps gTLD
applicants understand whether a proposed
gTLD string may be at high risk of name
collision before they submit an
application.
Name collision occurs when a name used
in a private network results in a query
to the public DNS.
If the name from the private network
matches a domain name in the DNS, it can
cause confusion and produce adverse
results.
Name collision risk is evaluated during
the string evaluation phase of the
application process.
If a string is identified as high risk,
the applicant may be required to develop
a mitigation plan, which can add cost,
time, and complexity to the application.
So, it's helpful to understand early if
your string is potentially at risk for
name collision.
The Name Collision Observatory does not
determine whether a string will pass or
fail evaluation.
It provides a database signal derived
from DNS query frequency to help
applicants understand whether a string
might present an elevated risk for name
collision.
The NCO aggregates data daily from
multiple sources.
This includes several root server
operators, as well as publicly available
data from two recursive DNS resolvers,
Cloudflare and QAx.
To use the tool, enter a proposed
string.
Internationalized domain name strings
may be entered directly or as punycode.
The NCO returns a magnitude score from 1
to 10 representing the relative
frequency of DNS queries observed for
that string.
To compare the string data to other
strings, click comparative stats.
The comparative magnitude data table
displays the magnitude score and score
rank for the most queried TLD strings,
whether delegated or not, on a specific
date.
The date is selected automatically based
on data availability for root server
operators and at least one weak cursive
data provider.
The magnitude score should not be
interpreted as an absolute risk rating.
Also, avoid cross-source comparisons.
Scores from one source are only
comparable with data from the same
source because the data contexts are not
equivalent.
The Name Collision Observatory is only
one of the tools available to help
assess name collision risk.
Potential applicants should not rely on
NCO alone and are encouraged to conduct
independent research as part of their
overall application preparation.
If you have additional questions, please
contact global support at
globalsupport@icann.org.

metadata.shortDescription:
Bald is Beautiful - September 17, 2026

Welcome back to DomainSherpa Review, the flagship podcast where experienced domain investors break down real domain sales, upcoming auctions, market developments, and the forces shaping domain name value.

In this episode titled “Bald is Beautiful,” JT is joined by Drew, Miller, and Dan Adamson for a wide-ranging discussion covering the next wave of new domain extensions, Verisign’s upcoming launch of .web, economic trends that could have a major impact on the domain market, and the recent MJ.com domain sale on RallyRd.

From evaluating domains like WellnessIQ.com, Clockify.com, Reversal.com, and Yono.com to looking ahead at changes in the broader domain landscape, the Sherpas dig into both individual domain values and some of the larger market forces domain investors are watching.

In This Episode:
1️⃣The Domain Game – Starts at 11:21. The Sherpas break down domain sales and guess what certain names were bought and sold for, explaining the reasoning behind their valuations. This week’s domains are WellnessIQ.com, Clockify.com, Reversal.com, and Yono.com. The Sherpas share their evaluations and discuss the factors they consider when determining what each domain may be worth.
2️⃣ NameJet Auction Review. The Sherpas review domains coming up for auction on NameJet, including Clack.com, DRCC.com, MedCard.com, and Pest.org. The Sherpas evaluate the names and discuss their perspectives on the upcoming auction opportunities.
3️⃣ The New ICANN gTLD Round & .WEB. The Sherpas get into where things currently stand with the new ICANN gTLD process and discuss Verisign’s upcoming launch of .web. The conversation looks at the continued evolution of domain extensions and one of the significant upcoming developments in the domain space.
4️⃣ Economic Trends & the Domain Market. The Sherpas discuss broader economic trends that could have a major impact on the domain industry. They explore the relationship between what's happening in the economy and what those developments could mean for the domain space.
5️⃣ The MJ.com Domain Sale on RallyRd. The Sherpas also discuss the recent MJ.com domain sale on RallyRd, adding another notable domain transaction to the conversation.
6️⃣ Dan’s Upcoming Move to Portugal. Dan Adamson shares details about his upcoming move to Portugal, giving the Sherpas another topic to dig into during the episode.
7️⃣ Sponsor: Appraise.net. Big news — Appraise.net is now a DomainSherpa sponsor.
8️⃣ DomainSherpa now integrates with Skiv.com (formerly Muse.ai), featuring searchable transcripts and an AI-powered video player so you can instantly jump to any topic, domain, or discussion point.
9️⃣ Watch all DomainSherpa episodes on DS.tv and stay plugged into the Sherpa Network.

metadata.title: How to Start A Top Level Domain Registry Business? Apply for New gTLD -2026 | ICANN New gTLD Program
metadata.author: Dotup ICANN Accreditation Consulting
metadata.shortDescription:
Thinking about investing in ICANN’s 2026 New gTLD round—or advising a brand on its own .brand? In this video, I break down how the program works, what it costs, where the real ROI comes from (security, trust, conversion, and distribution), and the exact steps from pre-application prep to launch. You’ll also see real-world adoption patterns, a de-risked budgeting model, and a field-tested playbook you can use with your finance, legal, IT/security, and marketing teams.

What you’ll learn
- New gTLD vs .brand (and why the best returns aren’t just “domain sales”)
- Application checklist: governance, technical RSP, trademarks/TMCH, and compliance
- Budgeting & timelines for the 2026 window (capex vs opex, where to save, where not to)
- Adoption playbook: security-first rollouts, phased DNS cutovers, and vanity-to-core migration
- Case-study takeaways from leading brands and why they scaled usage beyond pilots
- Investor lens: moats, risk factors, and exit paths across registry, registrar, and aftermarket
- How to evaluate RSPs, SLAs, data escrow, and ongoing policy obligations

Chapters
00:00 Intro & why this matters
01:32 New gTLD vs DotBrand (definitions you can use in the boardroom)
04:58 Cost model & 2026 timeline (capex/opex, hidden line items)
09:45 Security & trust ROI (phishing reduction, user journeys)
13:27 Case studies & quick wins
17:10 Risks, safeguards & compliance must-haves
20:42 Go-to-market rollout plan
24:30 FAQ + next steps

Work with me
I help enterprises and investors plan, apply, and launch their .brand / new gTLDs—end to end from strategy to first live domains. To discuss your 2026 plan, contact: venky@newgtldprogram.com

segments.text: How to use Archive.org to Analyze Expired Domains In this video, I will talk about my practical
experience of using the web archive to analyze expired domains that I buy through auctions.
Analysis at Archive.org is the most important step in studying the quality of domains before buying.
If you are subscribed to my channel, you can find videos on the rest of the work on searching,
analyzing, and buying expired domains. I’ve left the links to those videos in the description.
I'll walk you through those simple but essential steps for working with Archive.org,
which are necessary for the qualitative
assessment of the domain, namely: 1. analysis of the domain history and
lifecycle of the domain by years and months 2. search for possible spam domain history
3. study of possible domain redirects - 301 and 302. What's the difference?
4. content quality of the expired domain 5. using a web archive to restore site content
6. lack of an archive index is a critical factor before buying a domain
7. a quick analysis of a web archive from the Spamzilla service
First, I want to tell you how I do the initial analysis of the domain
before buying it at auction. 1. I search in Spamzilla and,
based on filters and sorting I find domains according to the given parameters, I
determine the most trustworthy domains for myself 2. I make sure to disclose information to SZ Score
about the domain where there is an Archive tab 3. In the Spamzilla service, I can see a few site
snippets with a domain life history, because it’s connected to Archive index. Yes, this is a very
modest sample, and the data is only sometimes up-to-date. By accessing Archive.org directly,
I will have a lot more data. 4. I watch all SZ Score tabs,
and if the initial assessment of the domain suits me, I do a link analysis in Majestic
5. The most important step in analyzing domain is the Archive.org
I will show an analysis of the https://www.kidneyurology.org/ domain
as an example of the Archive.org’s analysis. This domain has now lost some rankings, but recently,
it was at the TOP for thousands of supplements-related search queries.
This is a very interesting example, and among my videos, you can find a video with Case study
for this domain. So you should get acquainted with it. The site was earning tens of thousands
of dollars for its owner every month. So, let's analyze the domain in Archive.org
before buying it. 1. Enter the domain
https://www.kidneyurology.org/. Next, look at the general timeline and see that the
site was founded in 2002. Very long story 2. But we are most interested in the last
months of the domain life in its original form because we want to understand at what
stage it was expired and whether the site was as strong as in its best years just before it became
expired or it was bought and sold by spammers 3. I find that the site last had its original
look in January 2022. Then on the Archive history calendar, I see a very active phase. Indeed,
in May 2022, the domain was bought at an auction, and a new Wordpress site was built on it. Active
work on adding content to the new site has begun. 4. By evaluating Archive.org's screenshots of the
site's previous life, you can see a lot of content that can be copied to the new site.
For what? The fact is that old content can be a trigger for Google to retain its original purpose.
5. Before copying old content to a new site - I usually just create new posts in WordPress.
Check if the content is published elsewhere. You don't want duplicates. You can do this
by selecting a phrase and searching for it on Google in quotes. Spamzilla 's Duplicate
Checker or Copyscape may also be useful. 6. The last months of the site's life before
it got the expired status can show the presence of redirects. Often sites become expired because the
owners redirect a domain to a new one and forgot to renew the old one. If such a redirect exists
for more than a year before the domain expires, this may permanently transfer backlinks SEO juice
to the new domain. Google representatives say this, but it's hard to say how much truth is here.
I wouldn't say I like buying domains that were in 301 redirects in the last year of their life, I
never buy domains without any
archive index, I never buy websites that was expired a few years ago because he
losts links like crazy while it’s expired 7. Another thing is the 302 redirect.
It is temporary. If I see one, I ignore it. After all, from the SEO point of view, it does not
affect the transfer of link juice to another site. 8. So, the analysis of this domain by years
and months shows that it was
not in the hands of spammers before 9. It is also important if the domain
was immediately put up for auction after it was expired. I love buying freshly dropped domains,
they still look original, and Google loves them Now imagine that you saw a spam content in the
domain history in the last months of its life. Then you see a new wordpress site
with Viagra content. In this case, immediately refuse to buy a domain. It has already been
bought and dropped by spammers. They do this when the domain is not effective.
Use the Archive.org in your work as an auction domain bidder.
In my course, I made lessons about working with archive.org and other
services for a comprehensive site analysis. Be sure to buy access to my course at a discount,
and you can make a big business buying expired domains to create money sites. If you need help
buying domains, book my online consultation and I will help you find domains to buy.
Subscribe to my channel, where I post the latest SEO techniques and reviews of affiliate programs.
In addition, I plan to lunch free online courses on the most relevant SEO methods. Stay tuned.

segments.text: When evaluating expired domains, two key
age metrics can reveal a lot about value
and history. Hi everyone, Jacob Hanley
here today with another video from
expired domains. In today's video, we're
going to be talking about two metrics
that you'll see here on expired
domains.com when you're searching for
your next domain that are very
important.
First one is way back age abby on
expired domains.com and then who is age
wbby onexpired domains.com. Way back age
abby onexpired domains.com refers to the
earliest year the domain had an archived
website on the internet archive i.e.
when it first had content online. Who is
age wy on expired domains.com refers to
how long the domain has been registered
from the creation date in the who is
record. Now that we kind of know which
is which, why do we care? Why does this
matter when it comes to domains? So,
generally older is better. Search
engines consider older domains more
trustworthy and they often have more
backlinks and authority. However,
discrepancies between way back and who
is ages can signal interesting twists in
a domain story and history. So, let's
break down a few scenarios and what they
mean and how these can combine and why
they matter for your next domain
purchase. So, there's four key scenarios
that this can be a combination of and
we're going to go through each one and
talk about what they mean and which one
you should be looking for. So, scenario
one, way back age old, who is age old?
This is the truly ideal scenario. This
means the domain has been registered for
a long time and it had a website up long
ago that was indexed and archived. In
other words, it's got a continuous
ongoing history. This typically implies
a stable domain that's been maintained
over the years without ever expiring.
Such a domain is more than likely to
have accumulated a lot of backlinks, a
lot of trust, and a lot of great SEO and
is a very seasoned domain. It also
heavily implies that the name was so
valuable and is so valuable that no one
ever allowed it to drop. Perhaps it's
been an established business. Perhaps
it's just a highv value domain in
general. This is usually the best combo
of the ages and aby and wy. Scenario
two, way back age old and who is age
new. What I'd call the reborn domain.
Here the way back machine shows the
domain had an active website years ago.
Old content history. But the current who
is registration date is recent. This
strongly indicates the domain expired
and dropped at some point but then was
reregistered by a new owner. The who is
birthday got reset. So in plain terms,
the domain had a life. It died, expired,
and was reborn under new ownership. This
scenario is a mixed bag for value. On
one hand, the old archive means there's
an existing backlinks and name
recognition, and it's been around for a
long time. But on the other hand, since
it drops, you have to ask why. Good

metadata.title: What Sales Settings to Choose When Selling Domains - Buy Now VS Make Offer
metadata.author: Sedo.com, LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Before you list your domains for sale you should understand what type of Sales Settings best suits your domains. Sedo allows you to sell domains listed as Make Offer and Buy Now. In this video we will talk about your options and which ones may be beneficial to your domain for sale listing.

Sedo recommends listing domains as "Buy Now" as our research shows that these domains are three times more likely to sell with a fixed price than a standard Make Offer listing.  You can also benefit from a reduced commission fee if the domain sells while being parked with Sedo and listed as Buy Now. This is how a Buy Now listing will look to potential buyers. 

Buy Now listings are transparent and eliminate potentially lengthy negotiations as buyers know exactly what you want to sell for right away.  Also, in order to qualify for our SedoMLS Premium Partner network promotion and instant domain transfers, one of the requirements is that the domain is listed with a Buy Now price. Check out our video what is SedoMLS and How to activate MLS Premium to see how this promotion can help you sell domains faster.

Another thing is that, psychologically a Buy Now prices create a sense of urgency for buyers; if they don’t buy now, they may lose out! For domains already listed on Sedo as Make Offer, if you have received offers on the domain already, you can set a Buy Now price, and all previous buyers who made offers will get an email encouraging them to buy the domain now that they no longer have to negotiate. So that can be used as a sales tactic to help you sell.

Buy Now is not the best option for you when you have not researched or understood the domains correct value. If your domain is listed for sale for the wrong price then having a high Buy Now price will put potential buyers off. If you don’t know how much to sell the domain for then, in order to provide you with maximum flexibility when listing domains we also offer the option to list domains as Make Offer. If you list a domain as "Make Offer", you are indicating that the domain is open to receiving offers. You can list the domain with no asking price or minimum offer and the domain listing will look like this to visitors. 

Make Offer is ideal for you if you do not understand the value of your domain, you can find out if there is any interest in the domain to start with and to see what offers you get. This listing Allows buyers to make offers of any amount over 20 GBP, Euro or USD. . 

Any price you list against you "Make Offer" domains is not binding and you can counter offer to any offer you receive.  By entering a Minimum Offer and a suggested asking price your listing will look like this. 

This type of listing will avoid you receiving low offers that you are not interested in and is more transparent to buyers giving them a clear idea of how much you want to sell for, you are not obliged to sell even at an asking price even if you get an offer of this amount. All offers over the minimum offer received are passed on to you by email for consideration. 
Don’t forget to subscribe to our videos so you don’t miss out on any new content we are releasing and keep watching for the next video where we will show you how to list a domain for sale in your Sedo account.

We wish you every success selling your domains.

Marketplace for domains.
WWW.SEDO.COM

metadata.title: A Buyer Offered Me $50,000. It Was a Scam
metadata.author: Domain Value Estimator
metadata.shortDescription:
A buyer offered me $50,000 for a domain. The offer never existed. This video shows the four moves of the oldest scam in domaining: the huge unsolicited offer, the appraisal condition, the fee, and the vanishing buyer. Then the five other costumes the same scam wears, what a real buyer actually does, and the one question that makes a fake buyer disappear.
In this video: the $50,000 offer, the appraisal scam documented by Namecheap in 2016 and Sedo in 2020, the $50 to a few hundred dollar fee, fake escrow look-alikes, the overpayment, the fake payment screenshot, the fake trademark threat, the fake renewal invoice the FTC warned about in May 2026, real Sedo sales from the live feed, the free appraisal check, and the five red flags.
One honest note: the $50,000 offer in the title is the pattern, told the way it arrives in your inbox. This video teaches the documented scam pattern from published warnings, not one specific email. No victim, no invented domain, no invented price.

Appraise any domain free (2 a day, no signup): https://domainvalueestimator.com
Recent domain sales (live Sedo feed): https://domainvalueestimator.com/recent-domain-sales
Expiring domains, AI scored: https://domainvalueestimator.com/expiring-domains
Pricing: https://domainvalueestimator.com/pricing

0:00 The offer
0:32 Fifty thousand dollars, for a twelve dollar name
1:49 The one condition that changes everything
3:17 Five costumes, one pattern
5:14 The question that ends it
6:49 The check that costs nothing

Welcome to the Kickstart Commerce podcast where we share search marketing and domain investing strategies to help grow your business.

In today's episode, our guests are Jason Eisler and Yogi Solanki. Jason Eisler is a long-time domain investor and broker, and the founder of DNAdvisor.com, a boutique domain brokerage agency aiming to help domain owners maximize domain sales and profits.

Yogi Solanki is a newly minted domain investor that has taken to the domain industry much like a fish to water, having dialed in and refined domain outbound marketing strategies leading to consistent weekly domain sales.

Today Jason, Yogi, and I discuss:

How they’ve approached and refined their outbound strategies and best practices to sale domains.

The best types of media, tools, days/times and more to realize efficient domain outbound marketing sales.

The 3 Rules of Engagement: Relationship, Education, and The Close.

In closing, don’t forget to subscribe as you enjoy this week's episode via iTunes, GooglePlay, Stitcher or how ever you desire to listen. 😍
 
Last but not least, please visit KickstartCommerce.com and DNAdverts.com to learn more about search marketing and domain investing ideas to grow your business.

metadata.title: Domain Valuation - How to Price and Sell Domains
metadata.author: GoDaddy
metadata.shortDescription:
Have you ever wondered what your domain name was worth? 

✅Read about it here ➜ http://bit.ly/2YBfLBwGoDaddy

Get your business online in minutes with GoDaddy Airo: https://social.godaddy/airogodaddy. 

It’s an important question that’s worth answering. Whether you have a domain that’s about to expire or an eager buyer contacting you out of the blue, knowing the importance of accurate domain valuation is key.

Are you sitting on an unknown fortune like some antiques at a roadshow? Do you have buyers interested in your domains? Are you an active investor with 600 domains, but simply don’t have the time to manually update and research pricing each time the market shifts? 

Up until now, you had a few standard options for pricing and selling domains — you could ask experts in the field and get some feedback on the value of your domain, you could use some of the free or paid online appraisal tools, or you could guess.

Since each domain is unique (e.g., car.com is different from MyCar.com or Cars.com in value), the task to differentiate the nuances of meaning can be daunting for a machine to parse. 

Thankfully, with the use of some of the latest technology and a wealth of sales data as the leading marketplace for domain names, GoDaddy developed a tool that leads the market in evaluating and appraising domain names.

Like everything else, the internet is a business. Just like you pay the post office to deliver mail, you pay internet registrars to deliver visitors to your web address.

GoDaddy Domain Name Value & Appraisal uses an exclusive algorithm that relies on both machine learning and real market sales data to estimate domain values. Now, you can get the most accurate and comprehensive domain pricing estimates available. It’s almost like having access to your own domain expert or antique appraiser right from your computer.

Once you know the value of your domain, you know how much you can sell it at auction or privately.
 
If you wish to sell it at auction, choosing a site with a lot of affiliates, like Afternic.com, gives your domain name the most visibility. 

If you have a good domain name, at some point you’re likely to get an unsolicited offer to purchase the domain privately. If you’ve used GoDaddy Domain Name Value & Appraisal ahead of time, you’ll have a good idea of the value it holds and whether or not the offer is on point.

At the end of the day, a domain name’s value is what someone is willing to sell it for.
We strive to provide fair market value (i.e., what we think the domain name should sell for in an open market) so that you can make educated decisions.

While the valuation tool can be very helpful, it’s also important to keep in mind that it is an automated tool. It’s essential when making any type of financial decision about either purchasing or selling a domain name that you look over the pricing and do some additional research yourself before making any final decisions.

The Journey is what everyday entrepreneurs, like you, need to follow in the pursuit of online success. Our experienced GoDaddy Guides are here to take you through all the steps, both big and small, that you encounter every day.

Twitter: https://twitter.com/godaddy
